speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. I wonder whether the minister could give the house any additional information with respect to the tragic accident which resulted in the death of Air Vice Marshal Keith Hodson.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DEATH OP AIR VICE MARSHAL HODSON
speechtext:
Air Vice Marshal Hodson was deputy chief of staff for operations at NORAD headquarters. Part of his duties required him to be cognizant of the problems connected

with flying jet interceptors in squadrons under the operational control of NORAD. At the time of the accident he was undertaking a proficiency rating in a T-33 jet trainer, and due to a flame-out of the jet engine both he and the other pilot, a U.S.A.F. colonel, parachuted from the aircraft. Air Vice Marshal Hodson's parachute opened successfully, but for causes which are still unknown he suffered fatal injuries. An investigation is now under way in an effort to establish the cause of his death.
Air Vice Marshal Hodson was a distinguished officer in the R.C.A.F. I would like to express to his family and his fellow officers in the R.C.A.F. my sincere sympathy on the occasion of his death in the line of duty.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member sent me notice of his intention to ask this question only a few moments ago. I have not had an opportunity to check the hon. member's allegations concerning reports which he said emanated from the senior officials of my department. I should like to advise him, however, that I am informed by officials of the Denison mines that a severe shortage of labour exists at the present moment at Elliot Lake. My officials in the national employment service are now

trying to fill an order for 50 miners who will be employed for a period of two or three years in the mines there, and I am also informed that another 50 will be required almost immediately. The type of personnel required is in the skilled rock breaker category. The existing shortage has cut capacity in the mine by 20 per cent.
Miners presently in the Elliot Lake area are being referred to these jobs, and every effort will be made to fill the present requirements.
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Is the minister aware that miners at Elliot Lake have accepted jobs in other areas at half the pay that is being paid in the Elliot Lake area?

Mr. Speaker, I know that some miners insist on moving into other areas and some are being paid by the government for their removal to these areas, even though there is an opportunity of procuring work in the Elliot Lake area.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON PROGRESS TOWARD INTERNATIONAL CONTROL FOR PEACEFUL USE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also have a reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Assiniboia on the same day. His question concerned the present status of the international discussions directed to the establishment of international safeguards on the peaceful uses of atomic energy.
The discussions referred to have been carried on in the board of governors of the international atomic energy agency, which is an international body operating under the auspices of the United Nations.
At the board of governors' meetings held last March and April a document was provisionally approved by a large majority of the 23 members which embodied proposals for a system of safeguards against the diversion to military use of nuclear materials supplied for peaceful purposes. It will be discussed this coming September by the general conference of the agency in which the entire membership of over 70 nations is represented. The force and effectiveness of any multilateral system of safeguards and the extent to which it can replace the bilateral controls now maintained by Canada and the other major suppliers will, of course, depend upon the general acceptance accorded to the proposal.
Up to the present time some members of the agency, and in particular the Soviet union, have not given the proposed system their full support. It is therefore of the greatest importance that the forthcoming debate at the conference of the 70 nations should result in a general and favourable endorsement of the proposals leading to their unanimous acceptance and early implementation by the board of governors.
Canada is a member of the board of governors and has strongly supported its efforts to develop a generally acceptable system of safeguards. In common with their other supporters, who include the world's major suppliers of nuclear materials, we believe that effective international safeguards, if they can be developed, will make an essential contribution toward the controlled disarmament which continues to be our objective.

Penitentiaries-
161.	Administration of the office of the commissioner of penitentiaries including $90,000 for grants to recognized prisoners' aid societies as may be approved by the treasury board, $641,516.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Just before the end of the discussion on another item, item 151, last Thursday I was asked by the hon. member for Megantic a question about the number of inmates or prisoners who had been freed under the royal prerogative, and I undertook to obtain the information. However, at the close of the exchange I said:
I take it the hon. member wishes to know how many pardons, conditional or absolute, were granted in the last fiscal year. I will get that figure and supply it.
On rereading the question asked by the hon. member I have concluded that what he was really concerned about was not the granting of pardons but the number of unconditional releases of inmates from prison under the royal prerogative of mercy as opposed to releases on parole.
During 1959 there were 175 inmates serving sentences under the criminal law of Canada who were released, prior to expiration of sentence, by the Governor General under the royal prerogative of mercy on the recommendation of the Solicitor General.

On the item before us, Mr. Chairman, may I say that I do not think even the building of new prisons will in itself accomplish very much in the field of rehabilitation or reform. Even when these new institutions at Valleyfield, Springhill and other
Supply-Justice
places are opened and in full operation there will still be a decidedly large number of inmates in Canadian prisons and we will still be faced with the problem of overcrowding unless this expansion of prison facilities, especially in the medium and minimum security field, is still further extended.
I believe we might consider this subject in the light of the remarks made by the minister and the thoughts he has-perhaps I could even say the hopes he has-in so far as the treatment of narcotic addicts is concerned. I do not differentiate between those who have been confined under the provisions of the narcotic act and those who have not, because efforts must still be made to treat them.
The minister referred to institutional treatment which would be provided, and I assume he had in mind treatment of a psychiatric type rather than physiological treatment, because apparently the major problem in connection with addiction is psychological. I think we shall need to rely on doctors experienced in the psychiatric or psychological field to do the major amount of work in this regard. The mere provision of medium and minimum security prisons in this country will not by itself effect the rehabilitation of this type of prisoner unless it is accompanied by an adequate program of treatment, and at the moment we are faced with a shortage of workers in the important field I have mentioned.
I made some inquiries of the minister in this regard, and the answer I received is printed in Hansard of February 23. I have the original typewritten copy of the reply dated February 23. In any event, I inquired of the minister how many psychologists and psychiatrists are employed on a full-time basis at each of the penal institutions under federal jurisdiction. In reply the minister gave information to the effect that there are a total of 11 psychologists stationed at institutions across the country at Dorchester, St. Vincent de Paul, Kingston, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, and that there are no full-time psychiatrists but that these services are provided on a part time basis at all institutions. In addition there are staff members who are classification officers with some training in psychology and social work who contribute something in this field in conjunction with the professional psychologists.
Unless parliament is prepared to spend more money on the employment of full-time psychologists and psychiatrists there will be little decrease in recidivism, and little improvement in rehabilitation. That is not an original thought but one often expressed by penologists.

Supply-Justice
Under the present system a person convicted in Ottawa would automatically go to the penitentiary at Kingston, and one convicted in British Columbia would be sent to New Westminster. There is an arrangement for the transfer of prisoners from one penitentiary to another, from maximum security prisons to training schools like that at Collin's Bay.
I suggest that when a person is convicted he be confined during a period in which he would be interviewed by a board consisting of penologists, psychiatrists or psychologists, who would decide to which institution the prisoner should be sent to achieve the maximum degree of rehabilitation and corrective training. Prisoner A, perhaps a first offender, might be sent to a training institution where he could learn a trade that would be valuable to him upon his release. Prisoner B, if not susceptible to learning, could be directed to some other institution where another type of training was available. A deeply disturbed person could be sent to an institution where he would receive the maximum amount of intensive psychiatric assistance.
It was the practice in the past to send prisoners to maximum security prisons with little attempt being made to segregate first offenders from recidivists, from the deeply disturbed or from those convicted of offences involving sexual deviation or perversion. This condition has been aggravated by overcrowding and the lack of full time psychiatric treatment. Some strides have been made in improving the situation, but a great deal more has to be done in this area.
I know the minister and his officials appreciate that it is not enough simply to provide more prisons if there is not an intensive expansion of psychiatric treatment and an enlightened approach. We must convince society to adopt a new approach to the problem. Prisons can no longer be viewed merely as places of isolation and punishment. Without a greater emphasis on rehabilitation and psychiatric assistance it will be another 50 years or more before we make any real progress in this important endeavour.

Mr. Chairman, I note that item No. 161 provides for grants to recognized prisoners' aid societies, and that this year the estimate shows an increase from $75,000 to $90,000. Would the minister be kind enough to tell us how we have arrived at this increase of $15,000 for this year? I would also like to know whether these societies submit a budget of their needs. If so, what was the amount they suggested for this year, and was any cut made in their request?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The agencies do submit financial statements to us, and they also submit reports on the amount of work they have done for us in the year just concluded. It is on the basis of the work they do, the number of cases they handle, that the division of the total amount authorized is made among the agencies.
With respect to the amount of the increase, I would not suggest that it is proportionate to any amount of work. We recognize the importance of the work done by these agencies for the prisoners and for the correctional system generally, and we are auxious to help them to the greatest extent possible. We have made an increase in each of the last three years. In 1955-56 the amount provided was $40,000; in 1956-57 it was $50,000; in 1957-58 and in 1958-59 it was $60,000. For this year we have increased it to $75,000.
As I say, we are anxious to give as much financial help as we can on the basis of the work done, but the limits of the amounts we can give are set by treasury board. I suppose the answer as to why we arrived at the increase of $15,000 might be said to be that this was all that treasury board would authorize.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to raise two small matters. One relates to something about which I wrote the minister, namely criticism of the annual report in connection with penitentiaries. I received an answer to the effect that the information carried in those reports was in a sense of a traditional character, and useful. I will not push the criticism again, but I should like to say that this is one of the ugliest and worst edited reports that I have encountered in the government service. I think it is loaded with information that does not need annual reiteration.
In his reply to me the minister indicated that there was information in the report which was very valuable. I quite agree. For example, I would not like to see any of the statistical tables dropped; but I suggest to the minister that the annual reiteration about a cook moving or of some change in the kitchen is not necessary. If this kind of petty administration detail was dropped, or if there was a general synopsis instead of this reiteration in each particular area of the country, we might expect a much better presentation of the statistics.
One of the tables that interests me is that indicating the ethnic background of prisoners. Why could we not have in the reports occasionally a recapitulation of this information back over a number of years? I am

shocked when I look at the annual report to see the very direct relationship between educational attainment and incarceration in penitentiaries. On occasion I should like to see in this report historical consideration of this relationship in statistical form, with some kind of analysis. Instead, we get in this report year after year, a repetition of what I consider to be supernumerary details.
I suggest to the minister that he look at some of the other departments of government which have smartened up the editorial work on their annual reports in recent years. If he looks at the annual reports in some kind of perspective and checks them back for four or five years, I do not see how he can be pleased with the ones put out. I see that these reports cost $7,000 last year, and it is estimated that they are going to cost $7,300 this year. It is not much money, but I think we could expect better editorial work for our money than we are getting.
I notice that the provision for the publication of reports of the Department of Justice for the coming year has dropped from $22,000 to approximately $2,500. I cannot very well retrace my steps, but I was quite interested in this and wondered whether it indicated that in the central administration of the department there was a complete revision of this attitude toward publications.
The second point I wanted to touch on related to something brought up recently by the hon. member for Laurier, namely the question of the prison farm being so close to or involved with the metropolitan area of Montreal. In one of our parliamentary committees we had a witness who has had a great deal of experience as a policeman with criminal elements across the country. In offering us some opinions as to the relative criminal milieu at Toronto, Montreal and other places, he made the point that he is always surprised that Montreal is not worse than it is because of this very large prison population feeding into and out of the city and in a sense being part of the climate of the city and the city a part of the climate of the prison. I would certainly gather from his judgment, and the hon. member for Laurier tended to argue the same way, that one of the best steps that could be taken with regard to the Montreal situation in terms of, let us say, criminal health, would be to remove the prison farm or the penitentiary farm from this city and put it in some kind of rural section. I do not know what would be involved in this in terms of expense, but certainly it was brought very close to all of us in that committee who heard this evidence of the close tie and relationship between the penitentiary and
Supply-Justice
the city, and it certainly brought to the mind of those of us from Ontario how fortunate Toronto and Hamilton have been in having Kingston penitentiary or Portsmouth in that section of Ontario.

I appreciate what has been said by the hon. member and also by the hon. member for Skeena. Perhaps the remarks of the hon. member for Skeena do not call for a detailed reply at this time. They will be kept in mind as we make our attempts to improve the penitentiary program generally. I can assure the committee that we realize that the best facilities are of no use unless we have trained personnel to manage them and to operate the program. We do have a problem in securing the personnel. I think that is all I should say on that point.
With regard to the annual report, I accept the criticism of the hon. member as something which will require investigation and study to see whether we can improve the report from the point of view of the knowledge it imparts and the convenience of the readers in acquiring that knowledge. However, I would point out to the hon. member something which he has perhaps overlooked. At the present time the Penitentiary Act itself requires that the reports from each institution be included in the annual report of the commissioner of penitentiaries. Maybe this is something we should look at when we revise the Penitentiary Act, but it imposes on us the obligation to include a lot of the detail which my hon. friend claims to be superfluous.

May I pose a question or two to the minister based on a matter which is in the detailed section of the estimates. I rather think that some of this information might more properly be referred to under item 162 or item 163, but I wonder whether we might not have a general understanding that we would deal with it all under one item.
We appear to be more concerned with the salvation of the souls of inmates than we are with their rehabilitation and the contribution we can make toward getting them to be better citizens once they are released. I notice on page 230 that eight part time psychiatrists are listed as compared with six last year but there are 17 full time chaplains plus two part time chaplains. I think some of the money provided for chaplains might be directed toward obtaining more psychiatrists and psychologists. In any event, I should like the minister to indicate two things to me if he can. With what regularity or upon what basis do psychiatrists visit prisons? Does this vary from one prison to the other? Do they only

Supply-Justice
attend when asked? Second, will the minister indicate where I can find the reference to psychologists under this vote or under some other vote, as the case may be? How are they classified? Are they called something else?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
To deal with the points in the order in which they were raised, may I say I do not want to get into a controversy with the hon. member as to the importance of the chaplain service to the penitentiaries, but I certainly would not accept any suggestion that the chaplain service is not an essential part of the organization and one that is essential to the welfare of the inmates. It may be that the hon. member was being a bit humorous. With regard to the comparison of numbers, I will confine myself to saying that there are chaplains available and frequently we find it difficult to obtain the services of psychiatrists.
The organization of the psychiatric service is on the basis of five half days per week. The psychiatrist attends regularly every morning or every afternoon Monday through Friday. A psychiatrist is also available at any time, of course, for consultation or referral should a special need arise. Psychologists are categorized as rehabilitation officers 7.
Are there other rehabilitation officers 7 who are not psychologists? I think there must be.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, there are. The number of psychologists is contained in the answer I gave the hon. member earlier in the session, to which he referred this morning.
May I suggest that in the future it would be helpful if the number of psychologists could be indicated in brackets.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We will be glad to consider that.

I have one other question relating to page 232 and the further details for construction, improvements and equipment. This matter may also be dealt with in the supplementary estimates, but I should like to ask a question with respect to St. Vincent de Paul. One of the series of questions I asked had to do with the number of cells in penitentiaries which did not contain toilet or wash basin facilities. The answer was that there are 107 in Dorchester penitentiary and 420 in St. Vincent de Paul. In other words, these cells are simply cement encased bare rooms with no toilet facilities whatever; yet inmates have to spend a considerable number of hours in such cells.
I imagine that the present toilet facilities perhaps consist of a bucket. That is what I have been told. Unfortunately I have not had a chance to visit St. Vincent de Paul yet, but I hope to do so. I understand that early

in the morning there is a bucket parade for the inmates of these 420 cells without toilet or wash basin facilities, and that the buckets are emptied in some central spot during the morning. What steps are being taken to eliminate cells without toilet or wash basin facilities at St. Vincent de Paul and Dorchester penitentiaries? There are a large number at St. Vincent de Paul and a relatively large number in comparison to the inmate population at Dorchester. There are also a few at Kingston, although the number there is relatively small.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
With regard to cells without toilet or wash basin facilities, I am glad to say that the 107 at Dorchester are not now occupied. There has been some slight reduction in the population there so that we do not have to use these cells now. When the move to Springhill is made, which should permanently reduce the population at Dorchester and give us some leeway to carry out works and measures of this kind, it is the intention to strip these cells and use the area for recreation and similar purposes.
With regard to St. Vincent de Paul, I regret that the situation there is not so fortunate. I have to report that the majority, if not all, of these cells are occupied. Because of the physical nature of the building, St. Vincent de Paul represents our worst overcrowding problem at the present time. However, as soon as l'lnstitut Leclerc is available for occupancy, which will be this fall, we will be able to move men over there and clear out this area. It is the intention to remodel that portion of the building then and use the space as a dormitory. Therefore by the end of this year or by next year, or as soon as it can be physically done, I hope we will not have in either of these institutions cells without toilet facilities; and if we have them I certainly hope it will not be necessary to use them.

I have one other thought I should like to express with reference to chaplains. It was not my intention to say they had no place in these institutions. However, I think it will be found that the church attendance of the inmate population is in a much higher ratio compared to total inmate population than is the case with any other group in society outside the penitentiaries. I think many prisoners look upon attendance at church service as a form of recreation, in that they can be free from the restrictions of their cells and chat with their friends and so on. To that extent church service is looked upon as more or less a form of recreation, yet we hope that by association they will also get some spiritual guidance.

Can the minister make a
progress report as to the discussions held with the provinces on the matter of taking into the penitentiaries all persons sentenced to serve a year or more?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am very sorry, but I did not get the full question the hon. member asked.

Last year there was a meeting of the Minister of Justice and the attorneys general of the provinces with a view to changing the law so that all prisoners sentenced to over one year would serve their sentences in a penitentiary instead of a county jail.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is correct; that conference was in the fall of 1958, and there was agreement on that principle. I have reported before on it. It is a part of the over-all correctional reform program on which the correctional planning committee has been working. The committee presented its report, which is before cabinet for approval in detail at the present time.
The intention is that in the future the whole program, both of physical construction, and of training and rehabilitation, will be based on the federal authority assuming responsibility for all prisoners sentenced to a term of more than one year. However, we have to solve our own overcrowding problem and get our own present responsibilities in satisfactory shape. We will not yet be able to undertake the expanded responsibility this would represent, and the attorneys general have been advised that it will be three or four years before we expect to be in a position to assume this responsibility, but our planning is based on that feature.

Is there an effort made to have all inmates seen by a psychiatrist reasonably soon after their admission, or are they examined only after they have become mentally disturbed and are referred by a medical officer?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, the initial interview is carried out by the classification staff with a psychologist. If there is an indication that the inmate needs psychiatric help, then he is referred to a psychiatrist.

Item agreed to.
162.	Operation and maintenance of penitentiaries including compensation to discharged inmates permanently disabled while in penitentiaries, $14,878,797.

There is a reference here to compensation to discharged inmates permanently disabled while in penitentiaries. Does this refer to inmates who have become
Supply-Justice
permanently disabled as the result of sickness? What is the amount of the payment under this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It would not cover the case of an inmate disabled through sickness. I am informed that it covers the occasional industrial accident or event of that nature.

Item agreed to.
163.	Construction, improvements and equipment, $2,353,840.
In the details for this item there is reference to $1,097,400 for a new institution in Quebec. Is this the Valleyfield institution?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is l'lnstitut Leclerc
which we expect to have completed this year.
I understand Valleyfield has been completed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. Valleyfield was a military camp to which we had to make modifications, and that was completed last year.
I wonder if the minister could give a report on the situation at the present time at Springhill?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The situation is that construction is nearing completion. All the necessary equipment is on order and some of it has been delivered, while the rest of it is in the process of being delivered. Staff training is nearing completion and we expect, if things go according to plan, to be able to have it ready for occupancy and start transfers within the next two months.
How many prisoners is it expected there will be?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Approximately 100.
What would be the number of employees during that period?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In the neighbourhood of 35. The actual number will depend on the nature of the program, whether it becomes an industrial training type of program or a farm operation type of program or a combination of both. I cannot give an exact figure for the staff until we determine the type of program that will be carried out.

Ever since being elected to this house in March, 1958 I have been quite interested in the construction of penitentiaries in western Canada. We have placed our views before the department with regard to the need for penitentaries in British Columbia. We have requested also that serious consideration be given to locating a penitentiary in the city of Fernie. I realize that the length of time taken in reaching a decision is excusable because of the investigation being

Supply-Justice
conducted into our whole penal system. The report of the investigating committee was turned over to the department in January of this year, but we are still waiting for some action by the department. In the meantime the community is endeavouring to carry on, hoping for an affirmative decision to build the penitentiary in Fernie.
In August, 1958, as recorded on page 3201 of Hansard, I brought to the attention of the department the tendency to centralize penitentiaries in the province. Hon. members agree that many of the larger industrial concerns in Canada have found that it does not pay to centralize too many departments in a small area, and I suggested that consideration should be given to spreading the penitentiaries around the province of British Columbia. At that time the need for something to stabilize the economy in Fernie was quite urgent. I mentioned that the mines had closed down almost overnight. In several other instances communities have been advised that the mines will close within two or three years, but in the case of Fernie the mines closed down overnight and the employees wiere advised there was no more work.
I was advised that a three-man committee would investigate various sites across Canada. I was very disturbed to learn that only one man went to the city of Fernie, and it appeared to me this was just a token effort to show that there was a certain amount of interest in Fernie. In 1959 I also brought this matter to the attention of the department, and at that time the need of the city of Fernie was greater than in 1958. I received the following reply from the minister as recorded in Hansard of June 24, 1959 at page 5100:
When we get the committee's report we shall be able to come to some final conclusion. As I have assured my hon. friend and others who have written me on behalf of Fernie on previous occasions, the suitability of that location will be most carefully investigated.
That I certainly appreciate, but it is over two years now since I first brought this matter to the attention of the department, and it is six months since the report was filed. I feel it is now time that a decision should be made. We have been depending in this area on certain assurances that we were to be given consideration, but I do not think we should go on forever with such assurances. The case of Springhill was much the same, although my sympathies are with all mining areas, but it was not very long before a decision was reached to build a penitentiary there.
The department has been written to giving further considerations for a correctional institution in the Fernie district, and according
[Mr. McFarlane.l
to a press report I have here we are still given the chance of having a prison built there. It says that a letter from the Minister of Justice to the Fernie chamber of commerce outlined preliminary plans for correctional institutions in British Columbia and said that he would be giving his personal attention to the question of Fernie being a possible site for further development. I also noticed a press report from Elliot Lake greeting the announcement that a $2 million reform institution was going to be established there. All we are asking is that we be given the same consideration as other distressed areas where mines have closed down.

Before the minister replies I want to congratulate the hon. member for Kootenay East for fighting for his constituents in this respect, and I know he has raised the matter on two previous sessions.
I am interested in this matter because it appears to be government policy to consider areas suffering from depressed economic conditions when they have to consider building new penitentiaries. As the hon. member mentioned, one has been built at Springhill and according to the press one is to be built at Elliot Lake. I think he has made out a good case for one in British Columbia in the Fernie area. I know the circumstances he has related, and I rise to give my wholehearted support as a colleague in another portion of the Kootenays.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the feeling of the hon. member for Kootenay East, and I wish I could give him the assurance he wants and for which he has worked so hard. But I would remind the committee that we are designing a national system of correctional institutions. The program we are developing will be nation wide and the new institutions, wherever and whenever built, have to fit in with the national plan. It has been made clear to all communities which have pressed for the construction of new institutions in their localities that we are not prepared to make a decision as to where a new institution forming part of this pattern should be located until we have the pattern itself developed and approved; because to make such a decision in advance of the establishment of the basis of the whole program might well distort the program.
It is true that the report has been in my hands since January, but in a program of this magnitude neither my department nor the minister is free just to approve this and say "Go ahead". It has to have cabinet approval, and it is a very bulky, far-reaching and important document. When I say bulky it is in two large volumes. I press my colleagues as much as I can, but you cannot just

drop everything else and deal with the correctional planning report. I expect that it will be dealt with as early and as expeditiously as possible, and then we will be able to make detailed decisions based on the recommendations of the committee.
I know the situation in Fernie and there are at least a dozen, if not more, similar communities in British Columbia all of whom have been pressing me for a penitentiary to be located in their community. I have not yet been able to satisfy any of them, and I know I am in the position that when a decision is finally made I will have one friend and probably upwards of 99 disappointed enemies. But that will be my responsibility ultimately, and I will have to make the decision.
May I mention one impression which might be created by the hon. member's remarks if I left it uncorrected. It is not our policy to establish reform institutions in depressed areas. Where a decision can be made to establish a new institution or to extend an existing one by the establishment of a satellite, and where the proper factors to be taken into account do make it possible to locate in a depressed locality, then we locate there. But we are planning for the future. Penitentiaries and correctional institutions are long term, almost permanent institutions, and I think it would be very unsound to take as the guiding factor the principle that they should be located in a depressed area, which we certainly hope will only be a temporary problem. We would not have a scientifically worked out program if that was the sole basis for it.
It is true that a new institution has been established at Springhill, where it coincided with an area which had first a disaster and then became a depressed area as the result of the closing down of the mines. But this is not a completely new institution such as the one in western Canada will be. This is a satellite to Dorchester, which was established in accordance with that part of the program which establishes minimum security institutions as satellites to existing institutions and as projects which will relieve overcrowding in existing institutions. It is not the sort of new type of institution which will be built in accordance with the total program when that program is developed.
In British Columbia we have established a satellite to the British Columbia penitentiary, just as we have at Springhill a satellite. The needs were assessed and the areas available were assessed, and the decision was made to establish that one at William Head on Vancouver island, in part because the buildings were available exactly of the type we wanted, 79951-0-366
Supply-Justice
and in part because, being a satellite of the present institution, we wanted it to be reasonably close for administrative purposes.

Before the item carries, I was pleased to hear the minister say that this program for building additional correctional institutions is being carried out on a long range basis. However, I would remind the committee that every province in Canada has a penitentiary with the exception of Alberta. While I am not making the claim that we have more people requiring correction in the province of Alberta, I think in the interests of economy the location of this proposed new institution should be considered in the central part of Alberta. It would save the government a considerable amount in travelling, because we have people in Alberta who are sent to penitentiaries in Prince Rupert, or to Vancouver, or even as far as Kingston, which all involves considerable expense to the crown.
I make a plea, of course, on behalf of the area in which I am interested. I sympathize entirely with the hon. member for Kootenay East, but I would remind him that trade conditions with Japan have somewhat improved conditions in his area and therefore some of the urgency of his plea has been lost. I did make representations to the minister, and I frankly admit it, on behalf of central Alberta because of its facilities for an institution, its excellent transportation services and the fact that the province of Alberta does not at this time have a correctional institution.

I have two or three other thoughts to mention. I know there are some members of the house who have undertaken on their own to visit some of the prisons, although the number of members who have done so is small. Bearing in mind the saying that one look is worth a thousand reports, in order that members may get a better understanding of the function and operation of the penitentiaries, perhaps on lines similar to those developed by the Department of National Defence, I suggest that something might be done to arrange for small groups of members to visit some of our penitentiaries and prisons under the auspices of the department in order that they may get first hand knowledge and a better understanding of the facilities which exist, including some of the facilities which would be better removed from our prisons such as solitary confinement cells, the crosses and arrangements for lashes and other things of that nature. It would also afford an opportunity of understanding the attitude of the prisoners themselves. I commend this suggestion for study by the minister and his department.

Supply-Justice
As I have said, I do not think the groups should be too large-perhaps they should not consist of more than four or five members- in order that the visitors might have a better understanding of these things. It might be a couple of years before a large body of members of parliament would visit these institutions, but when they had done so they would be in a better position when the estimates were being considered to determine whether or not a correct approach was being made.
Another thought I have is in the form of a question. I believe that last year an officer or guard at Kingston was arrested for possession of narcotics. Presumably it was felt that he was not using those narcotics himself but was smuggling them into the prison. I wonder whether the minister could indicate what experience his officials have had in so far as attempts to smuggle narcotics into federal institutions are concerned, and perhaps we could be told the experience with regard to alcohol and other things of that nature. Is this practice prevalent or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The suggestion made by the hon. member for Skeena with regard to visits by members of parliament is one that should perhaps be studied. The question involved is, of course, whether the government should undertake responsibility for making buses available and paying transportation costs in connection with such visits. That is one of the things that will have to be considered. Also, since in many cases the institutions are close to Ottawa, particularly those at Kingston and Montreal, it is not really a great undertaking for members themselves who are interested, as I know the hon. member is, to visit these prisons on their own initiative, as I know the hon. member has done. However, we could give consideration to the question of visits by organized groups of members. We have no buses in the department, but perhaps the Department of National Defence would make its buses available to us. That is something we shall be glad to consider.
With regard to smuggling narcotics or other articles into prisons, this is something against which we have to be on guard at all times. However, our experience is that safeguards can be made effective and that our measures can be reasonably successful. I do not claim for a moment that narcotics or alcohol are never smuggled into prison, but the exceptions are, I think, rare enough that they do not warrant any cause for concern that our precautionary measures are not proving successful.
There was an incident in British Columbia recently where an ex-inmate had attempted to conceal narcotics. He was apprehended,

the cache was discovered, and there is a prosecution now under way. We had another case at Kingston where a guard was involved. Suspicion was aroused, an investigation was made, and as a result the guard has been dismissed from service.
I do not say those are the only incidents which have taken place recently, but when the British Columbia incident took place I did become concerned and asked that both the penitentiaries branch and the R.C.M.P. should let me have a report as to whether there was an increase in the incidence of smuggling of narcotics into penitentiaries. After examining their files and records and making an on the spot check, both organizations informed me that the situation in this regard was normal and that there was no indication either that our methods were unsuccessful or that there was any carelessness on the part of the staff of the institutions.
I understood the minister to say with respect to the guard at Kingston that he was dismissed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Does the minister know whether any charges were laid with respect to the possession of narcotics?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My recollection is that he was charged but acquitted for insufficiency of evidence or some such reason. I can send the hon. member the information as to the reason, but we would have to look it up in the files.

It just seems odd that a person should be dismissed because he was in possession of narcotics, presumably on fairly definite proof that this was the case, and then that the charge against him should be dismissed because of insufficient evidence. It seems to me there is a conflict between these two circumstances, and perhaps the guard would have the right to reinstatement if it was not proved that he was in possession of narcotics.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I can assure the hon. member that such was not the case at all. I said the charge failed for lack of evidence or some technicality. I am not sure what the technicality was. It was certainly not proven that the guard was not in possession of narcotics. The criminal charge did not succeed on some ground, some technical objection which was raised, as I recall it, by the defence. I will obtain information about the precise reason why the charge was dismissed and send the hon. member the details so he may be satisfied that we do not go about unjustly dismissing our guards.

Mr. Chairman, my only reason for rising is that when my constituents read today's Hansard and find that my colleague, the hon. member for Wetaskiwin, is the only Alberta voice that has spoken out in the house with respect to the proposed new penitentiary-my constituents are highly intelligent; they read Hansard-they may feel we are not fulfilling our duty if we do not participate. I think the minister knows that with respect to the proposed penitentiary in the west, as applied to Alberta, there is only one place for it and that is in southern Alberta.
My colleague from Wetaskiwin talks about travel. What that has to do with the inmates of a penitentiary I do not know. We in the south have railways, we have an excellent climate, we have occupations. We have all the conditions necessary for a splendid site for a penitentiary. I am sincerely persuaded that when the new penitentiary site is selected it will be somewhere in the southern part of Alberta.

Mr. Chairman, I am sorry I did not get the floor before the hon. member for Medicine Hat. Medicine Hat has nothing to offer compared with what I am going to propose in a few moments. I am speaking here on behalf of the town of Wainwright. I wish to draw to the attention of the committee and the minister the fact that this town is on the main line of the C.N.R., a terminal point where the continental train stops twice daily. Furthermore, the dominion government at present owns a large tract of land around Wain-wright. It is used for military purposes part of the year, but we could use this land as a site on which to build the penitentiary. We have an abundant supply of water from the river, natural gas and all the prerequisites for a site for a penitentiary. I am sure the minister and his officials will give Wain-wright every consideration when they are selecting the site for this penitentiary in Alberta.

Mr. Chairman, after listening to the remarks of my colleagues I can see that every hon. member wants this penitentiary to be located in his constituency. I merely want it to be located in Alberta. I know that in addition to these few spokesmen from whom we have heard today the minister has been badgered by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson and the hon. member for Acadia. When the minister has that fearsome combination of the Horner brothers confronting him I know he will have a difficult task. Therefore I feel I should simply 79951-0-366i

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister whether there is any danger on his part of being unable to choose between these idyllic communities in Alberta and having to move right out of the province?
The choice is going to be a difficult one, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, would the minister give us information about the work undertaken by the R.C.M.P. laboratories at Regina, which I believe do all research and analysis work for the force in western Canada? I am informed by officers there that large sums of money are spent in travelling expenses by individuals at Regina because of the necessity of their giving evidence in court. I am also told the time has long since passed when a laboratory should be established in the vicinity of Vancouver. At present the work from British Columbia must be sent to Regina, entailing some loss of time. An even greater loss of time is involved in members of the Regina staff travelling to British Columbia to testify in court. I am told that one or two of them spend more time travelling by plane to courts in British Columbia than they spend in the laboratory at Regina. Would the minister tell us What study has been made of the situation, and whether any thought has been given to the establishment of a laboratory in British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the matter of a further laboratory for western Canada is now under consideration. There have been

Supply-Justice
correspondence and discussions with the attorney general and his department in British Columbia with respect to the matter of the establishment of a laboratory, probably in Vancouver. That question is under study.
The hon. member is quite right when he refers to the problem created by the necessity of members of the staff flying from and to Regina to give evidence with respect to the exhibits analysed in our laboratory. As against that, the problem that has to be considered is the considerable expense of starting another laboratory because of the expensive equipment it requires. At the moment I can only say that the matter is under study, and it is under study on the basis that we recognize that there are compelling reasons arguing for the establishment of a further laboratory.

My remarks will be more restrained than last year because the situation then obtaining in Newfoundland has changed. I should like to make some comments about the activities of the R.C.M. Police in investigating allegations that a number of Chinese people have come to Canada illegally in the past few years, and the manner in which the investigation was conducted. I am given to understand that in the city of Vancouver, somewhere around the end of May, the R.C.M. Police executed 15 search warrants. Whether those search warrants applied to individuals or establishments I do not know. In any event, the homes and business establishments of the individuals concerned were in effect raided on the grounds that a conspiracy existed to bring Chinese to Canada illegally. I am given to understand that the R.C.M. Police seized documents which obviously had nothing whatsoever to do with any such alleged conspiracy, real or imagined.
Commissioner Harvison is supposed to have made reference to 11,000 Chinese coming to Canada illegally. This statement cast doubt upon the legal position of all members of the Chinese communities in Canada, because reference was made to no specific locality. I do not know what the situation is today, but weeks after the raids were carried out by the R.C.M. Police no indication has been given as to whether any charges would be laid or whether any of the documents seized would be returned. There has been refusal on the part of the R.C.M. Police to say what has happened with respect to the documents seized, and a cloud of suspicion has been cast upon the people involved in the search warrants.
I think some fundamental freedoms of the individual are involved here. The R.C.M. Police should have been more judicious in

their activities in this field. They should not have been so flamboyant in their attitude toward the public as to what they were doing. This has cast a cloud over the entire Chinese community in Canada. At the end of the raid no indication was given that any charge would be laid.
Furthermore, I am given to understand that some indication has been given-and this is reported to have come from the commissioner's office, though it may have come from the members of the R.C.M. Police- that the police do not intend to charge all the Chinese who have allegedly entered Canada illegally. If they do not intend to charge all, then this smacks of some sort of discrimination, the picking and choosing of people, if there are any who have come here illegally.
Then there is reference-and this I submit is the sort of red herring that is dragged in occasionally to cloud the issue-in the Vancouver Sun of January 8 to the fact that the R.C.M. Police had reported that red agents or communist agents-the story said "red"- have been brought into the country from China as part of the conspiracy. It seems that the R.C.M. Police are prejudiced toward looking for communists operating in Canada.
Another part of this unfortunate situation is the injudicious use of the R.C.M. Police in these raids and the manner in which the raids were conducted. These raids were widely publicized, and they cast doubt and suspicion upon each and every individual of Chinese origin who has come to Canada in recent years. These things should be cleared up immediately. If there are charges to be laid, lay them as quickly as possible and clear the air of the doubt and suspicion that rest in the minds of those people.
This situation was further aggravated in the city of Prince Rupert. I received a telegram from Mr. Bruce Brown, a lawyer in that city, inquiring what right the R.C.M. Police had to question citizens of Chinese origin about this matter. I checked and discovered that they had no right whatsoever, other than the normal right of a policeman to ask questions which individuals are not obliged to answer. I understand the people were advised accordingly and that they refused to answer the questions. It was not a matter of the R.C.M. Police constables or officers conducting the inquiry in Prince Rupert going to an individual Chinese in his home and telling him privately that he would like to ask a number of questions; it was a matter of asking the members of the Chinese community to report to the police station in the city hall to answer a number of questions.

I have a copy of the questionnaire provided for that purpose. I understand this questionnaire was developed somewhere in the regional offices, and its purpose was to ensure that the well-trained police constables did not miss anything in their interrogation. The information they required, without giving any indication what it was for, was the name and other names, addresses, business address, date and place of birth, occupation, distinguishing marks, tattoo, and so forth. There is reference to whether the person speaks English well or poorly, place and date of entry into Canada, name used at that time. He is asked whether he is a Canadian citizen, the number of the certificate when issued, issued in the name of; name of the sponsor and relationship, his address; whether the individual has a passport; what is the number of the passport; details about wife or wives or husband; about names; place and date of birth; number of children; place of birth of parents, brothers and sisters; production of all documents showing number of names, and so forth; previous address in Canada. If this sort of thing does not smack of the same sort of inquisitorial approach connected with the other raid which was conducted previously, I do not know what it is.
Second, I understand that a visa fraud section has been set up by the R.C.M. Police for which this sort of information is required in a sort of general way, indicating that everybody must answer the questions. This immigration visa fraud section has an unlisted telephone number; at least when you telephone them you find that it is not an R.C.M. Police number, it is another number. They do not answer by saying "R.C.M. Police"; they answer by saying "Hello" or something of that nature. If this is some sort of a secret organization that has been established in this regard I think the Chinese people should insist on their rights and refuse to answer any such questions, especially when they are asked to come down to the police station, as they were in the city of Prince Rupert, in order to be asked for information of this nature, namely whether a person has a passport; what other names he has; what information he has about brothers, sisters, parents, children, wives and husbands and all the other relatives that an individual may have. I think this is another of the erroneous steps the R.C.M.P. have taken in dealing with this question.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on this item, which concerns the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Along with every other Canadian I am proud of the record of the force; not only their
Supply-Justice
record on the television screen, though I have no particular complaint to make about that, but their record in history and the contribution the force has made to the growth, development and security of our country. The police, as is the case with every other police force, often have unpleasant duties to perform. No doubt our R.C.M.P. have their share of these. They also have the responsibility under the government for certain security duties which are not likely to make them very popular, but as far as my own experience goes I cannot imagine security police, doing the kind of things that have to be done and conducting these operations more fairly and discreetly and with a greater regard for the rights and liberties of the subject than our own security officers of the R.C.M.P.
Therefore, feeling as I do, and I think most Canadians feel the same way, we must all be very sensitive to any kind of unfavourable publicity that may attach to the force. There was unfavourable publicity a year or so ago. I am not going into that now because I think I would be out of order in any event, but it resulted as we know, in the resignation of the commissioner under circumstances which I think were regretted by everybody. This perhaps gives me the opportunity to pay my respects to the new commissioner, who I know will be a worthy successor to a long line of distinguished Canadians who have held that post.
The hon. member who preceded me referred to the unfavourable publicity which the R.C.M.P. has been getting in connection with one matter, that of Chinese immigration. There is no doubt that when announcements are made on a matter like this by the R.C.M.P. or by somebody speaking for the R.C.M.P. there will not only be publicity, but in a situation such as this there will be controversial publicity. I think that is unfortunate and regrettable. In my view the original announcement by the R.C.M.P., as reported by the Canadian Press on May 24, was regrettable in that such an important statement, which was bound to have repercussions and create controversy, should have come from someone authorized to speak for the government. The matter could then have been discussed on the floor of the house, because parliament was sitting. But when the commissioner makes an announcement in terms which suggested that 11,000 Chinese entered Canada illegally during the last ten years, that is bound to lead to misunderstanding and controversy, especially as in this case there has been no subsequent information that I have been able to secure from any governmental source which would confirm that that figure was any more than an estimate.

Supply-Justice
The announcement also included other things which were bound to create uneasiness in a segment of our population which, by an announcement of this kind, would feel itself to have been put under suspicion. There was another story in the Ottawa Citizen a few days later attributed to the commissioner of the police which dealt with the same matter; in fact it almost seems like the same story. These announcements have created a situation where the police have been brought into public controversy, and that is something which I think is regrettable.
The reaction and feeling in a certain section of our population-I am referring primarily to the Chinese section of our Canadian population-have been increased by statements made by a representative of the police on television. These statements may be perfectly accurate; I am in no position to judge, but having seen one program I feel that it was not the kind of program to keep the R.C.M.P. out of controversy.
The result of all this has been what one could have expected. Chinese Canadians have understandably felt resentful that some of the implications of these statements as having conveyed a reflection on the Chinese community as a whole, although I am sure not by design on anybody's part. As the minister knows, there have been complaints and representations by citizens of the Chinese race in Canada as a result of the statements made and their implications, and the R.C.M.P. have been brought into controversy. I am not going into the details of these submissions, but they have been made to the government. The minister has replied to some of the statements made, denying them, but the statements are on the record and they do include what I think are unfortunate references to the R.C.M.P., references of a kind that underline my own view, which I am sure is shared by others, that the police should be very careful not to become involved in the kind of situation which may result in that type of submission.
One statement I have here is found in the Toronto Globe and Mail of June 4. In it the Chinese community centre association say they resent strongly the widespread raids by the R.C.M.P. into their houses and places of business and so on. These have been denied by spokesmen on behalf of the government, but it seems to me that if the R.C.M.P. had refrained from making the original statement about 11,000 illegal entries they might have been in a stronger position in respect of subsequent statements and submissions that were made which reflect on the conduct of the police.

I should like to ask the minister, as I think the hon. member who preceded me also did, to give the committee some information regarding the activities of the R.C.M.P. in checking into illegal entries from Hong Kong. In answer to questions in the house the minister has already dealt with some aspects of this matter. In one of his statements he said that they, meaning the government, were making use of the service of some members of the Hong Kong police force who have been sworn in as special members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. He went on to say that they had been very carefully instructed in Canadian police methods and in the law regarding the carrying out of investigations and the questioning of individuals.
Now, all that is quite true, but the actions of the police in this connection, assisted by police officers from Hong Kong, however carefully instructed, are bound to create and have created in some quarters a feeling of resentment and anxiety. Perhaps the minister could take advantage of this opportunity to enlarge upon statements he has already made. This may serve, I would hope, to remove some of this anxiety and also to remove any reflections which may have been cast on a large body of Canadians. He might also deal with the question of the desirability of any representative of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police making a statement of the kind made, no doubt, in good faith and with good intentions, but which in connection with a matter of this importance and of such a controversial nature should come from a spokesman of the government itself.

speechtext:
