I do ask members, therefore, to bear in mind the fact that some of the things that are said are said obviously for this purpose. I do not mean they are said by members here, but some of the things that have been said outside have been said because nothing would better serve the interests of the racketeers than to have the Hong Kong police withdrawn. In order that this might be done we are told the Hong Kong police are brutal; that they have been carrying out their investigations and questioning in an entirely improper manner. We have investigated all allegations and have found them to be completely unfounded.
Therefore it is obvious that the allegations have at least one motive; that is, to try and force us, by creating prejudice against the use of the Hong Kong police, to discontinue their services. We have no intention of discontinuing their services, because their services are essential and are proving extremely valuable in assisting to uncover this racket.
The same thing is true with respect to the charges which have been made against the R.C.M. Police themselves in the course of carrying out these investigations. If the police could be prejudiced in the minds of the public, then the government presumably would tell them to take the pressure off, to ease up on the investigations and let the whole thing die. We have investigated every charge made against the R.C.M. Police and have found there is no allegation which need be taken seriously, except one relating to the use of the questionnaire, and I will deal with that separately. But as to the conduct of the investigations, the allegations that people have been haled out of their beds and homes in the small hours of the morning and practically dragged down to headquarters for questioning are entirely unfounded, and I say that on the basis of the most careful check on the circumstance about which the allegation was made. I am referring to a case in Montreal.
With respect to Prince Rupert and the use of the questionnaires, it is true the questionnaires were prepared, and they were prepared for the guidance primarily of the R.C.M. Police themselves. I am sure the hon. member for Skeena, who raised the matter, will appreciate that where you are dealing with a nation-wide investigation into the operations of an organized racket which itself is nationwide, then it is essential that all information should be collated. In order to make certain that the operation is successfully and expeditiously carried out it is essential that the same particulars be received in each case, that the same questions be asked of each

person being questioned. It was for this purpose that a form of questionnaire was prepared for the use of the police officers in conducting their interviews.
In Prince Rupert, as in other cities, the R.C.M. Police are carrying out investigations concerning this matter, and they have been provided with the form. The form was designed at headquarters as a guide for the use of members of the force during the questioning of persons who are voluntarily prepared to give a statement as to their status in Canada, and in carrying this out obviously some uniformity is a necessity. That is the purpose of the form.
As far as Prince Rupert is concerned, my information is that 11 members of the Chinese community were interviewed. Some of these were merely asked for advice as to the best approach to make to the local Chinese. Of the 11, only six were interrogated and only one supplied the answers and signed the form. The form was also shown by members of the force to the legal adviser of the local Chinese community. It is not a secret document with which they were suddenly confronted and asked to sign. Only one signed it, and only six were interrogated on the basis of the questionnaire.
I have made it clear, in case there was any lack of clarity, that the questionnaire is not to be used for the purpose of getting the Chinese to sign but only as a guide to interrogators in asking their questions.
Some objection seems to be taken to the fact that we are interviewing Chinese at all. As I say, we ask them if they are prepared to give information voluntarily; if they are not, then that is the end of the matter. But how could we conduct an investigation if we did not interrogate people and ask them for information? Of course we have to interrogate them, and interrogate them all across Canada, in some cases on the basis of information arising out of the documents seized and in other cases in the hope that we will get information from them which will enable us further to identify and establish and prove, and bring home the proof, that individuals are involved in this illegal racket. The interrogations must continue, but I again assert that every case of complaint which has been made has been investigated and will continue to be investigated.
I do not take the position that a mistake can never be made, and I am prepared to investigate every complaint that we receive. If there should be improper conduct we will deal with it; but these complaints so far made against the R.C.M. Police and the Hong Kong police, with the exception of the one incident

regarding the use of the questionnaire where a Chinese was actually asked to sign it-and that was not the intention for which it was designed-have proved to be completely unfounded.
The suggestion was made that there is concern and doubt in the minds of the Chinese community. I regret profoundly, in the same way as has been expressed by my colleague the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, that this investigation should have proven necessary. I regret profoundly that a substantial number of Chinese Canadians are involved in one way or another, and I can quite understand the reason for their general concern.
But on one point there should be no doubt, and I have done what I can to remove the doubt from the minds of those with whom I have discussed it by way of interview, delegation or in statements I have made in the house, and that is that there will be prosecutions. This racket does exist; we have evidence that it exists, and we have evidence on the basis of which I am assured with confidence that charges can and will be laid. So there should be no doubt in the minds of the community on that point; guilty persons will be charged and prosecuted.
I refer now to persons who are guilty of operating an illegal racket. I am satisfied that when that is established and the Chinese community know that so far as we can we will get these racketeers off their backs, then the feeling of the Chinese community will be one of relief and satisfaction.
In this connection I want to read an extract from a paper entitled "Our Sunday visitor", the issue of June 19, under the heading "Chinese suffer 70 year old tragedy". There appear these two opening paragraphs:
When mounted police recently began raids on Chinese homes and offices across Canada, it was the latest act in a tragedy that began more than 70 years ago. The police were looking for evidence to convict blackmailers who have played monstrously on the urge of the Chinese to come to an empty land across the Pacific and the recoil of the whites who got here first.
The crime committed was not merely one of illegal entry-that is little more than a technical fault. The real evil has been the ruthless exploitation of Chinese dreams. The blackmailers have been cruel and greedy and have grown rich over the years.
Our investigations to date establish that point. We have, as I said, gathered a substantial amount of evidence to date as a result of the documents we have seized. We are also receiving confessions from Chinese. We are now receiving the co-operation of the Chinese community in this investigation, and it is our hope that co-operation will be even more forthcoming. It is also my belief 79951-0-367
Supply-Justice
that it will be, when charges are laid and when it becomes evident in the clearest manner possible that our intention is to convict racketeers and not to prosecute or harass people who have, in many cases, committed no more than a technical offence many years ago. That has already been made clear by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration in her statement, and I think it will become more abundantly clear when the prosecutions commence. Then I believe we shall receive increasingly the co-operation of the best elements of the Chinese community so we can clear up this racket and dispose of it once and for all.
The hon. member for Skeena referred in addition to a couple of other matters. He said it had been reported in the Vancouver Sun that the R.C.M.P. had said that red agents had come into this country under cover of this illegal immigration. I am advised that this is not correct. The R.C.M.P. made no such statement, because they have no information of that nature. I am sorry the story was not picked up and contradicted immediately it appeared in the paper. I am informed also that the police never said they were concerned about red agents coming in during the course of this illegal racket.
The hon. member also expressed concern arising from a statement which he said the R.C.M.P. had made that some people would be prosecuted while others would not. He said this indicated to him that there might be discrimination. May I point out that the decision as to prosecution is not one for the R.C.M.P. to make. There are two things involved here. First there is the operation of an illegal racket. There is no question but that everyone concerned and exposed there will be prosecuted. The other matter is the situation of those who came into this country under false identities. The decision whether to prosecute in these particular cases is not one for the R.C.M.P. It is one for the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, and the minister has made her stand clear as far as the Chinese are concerned who were what I might call innocent passengers in this vehicle. We are after those who operated the vehicle itself. The decision as to prosecution in individual cases will be made by that department.
I think that covers most of the points raised. While I very definitely want to leave in the mind of the committee no possibility of misunderstanding as to our intention to continue this investigation and press it to the limit of every resource at our disposal, and to prosecute those who are thus exposed-I want to make that very clear so the racketeers will not be able to tell the innocent Chinese, "You

Supply-Justice
had better keep quiet, because nothing is going to come of this"-I want also to assure the Chinese community that something is going to come of this, because to the best of our ability we want to get these racketeers off their backs. I want to assure the Chinese community of our deep sympathy that they should be involved in this situation, and of our desire to clear it up so they can go about their lives without fear or worry.

The minister has taken exception to my using the word "announcement". I used that word not in any sense to mean a formal, voluntary statement by the R.C.M.P. If that is the meaning the minister has given to it, I can understand his feeling and I am very glad to withdraw the word "announcement". But the press is not as skilled in semantics as the minister is, because whatever may have been the circumstances surrounding the statements made by the R.C.M.P. in connection with the matter, they have been referred to in the press as statements; statements at a press conference, if you like, but nevertheless statements from the R.C.M.P., as the first statements which were made following the announcement last January, they led to the kind of publicity which caused so much trouble. This was due mainly to the use of the figure 11,000.
Let me justify what I have just said when I spoke about statements. The Canadian Press story, which is the one that circulates from coast to coast, under a dateline of May 24, reads:
R.C.M.P. Commissioner C. W. Harvison estimated that the ring made it possible for about 11,000 Chinese to enter Canada illegally during the last 10 years. This figure represents more than half the 21,000 Chinese admitted in that period.
That was the original story. That was the first time numbers were used, as far as I know. If you like, that is not an announcement, but it is a statement made by the commissioner in reply to a question and confirming that 11,000 Chinese had entered Canada illegally.
On June 2 a story appeared in the Ottawa Citizen purporting to be an interview with the commissioner of the R.C.M.P. Asked whether he agreed with the estimate that between 50 per cent and 85 per cent of Chinese immigrants had used fraudulent documents, he said-and this is in quotation marks-
I think that 85 per cent is probably a little high. Our evidence indicates the majority came in that way.
So the information that came from the R.C.M.P. in the form, if you like, of answers to questions was bound to be made public once it confirmed, if it did not volunteer, the information that 11,000 Chinese had entered this country illegally.
[Mr. Fulton.l
I have a great many other clippings on this matter in which occur such phrases as "the commissioner said" or "the commissioner stated". One from the Montreal Star of June 22 says "The news from R.C.M.P. headquarters that 11,000 Chinese-" and so on. Therefore I think my point is a valid one. If the R.C.M.P. as a force is to remain aloof, as we think it should do, from a controversy of this kind, then it should not make through its spokesmen statements which are bound to be controversial and, indeed, sensational.
The minister said no statement was made by any representative of the R.C.M.P. with regard to the security aspect of illegal entry. It is just as well that the minister is able to deny that, as I think he has done before, because here again in this story in the Ottawa Citizen the commissioner is reported as replying to a question put to him on this subject. This story, dated June 2, contains the following paragraph. The commissioner was asked if it would be fair to assume that any type of security risk could have been included in the illegal flow of immigrants, and his answer is given, in quotation marks, as follows:
"Yes, because of the high percentage it is obvious any could have been schooled for any design in seeking entry."
The point I am trying to make, and I think it is a valid one, is that if the R.C.M.P. is to be kept out of these controversies, statements of this kind are not the best way to bring about that desirable result. The minister said that the R.C.M.P. as a force has the respon-sibiilty for deciding whether to give information or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Whether to answer questions or not.

As a principle, of course, I do not take exception to that, because there will undoubtedly be times when information should legitimately be given to the press by the R.C.M.P. But this kind of information, which converted what up to that time had been a not very sensational announcement by a representative of the government into something quite sensational because of what amounted to confirmation of the figure given of 11,000 illegal immigrants, is bound to cause controversy. When a statement of that kind is supplemented by television interviews, then it seems to me that the force is being brought unnecessarily into a controversial situation and acquiring a kind of publicity which will not do it any good.
Those of us who are anxious that this should not happen to the R.C.M.P. have, I think a legitimate reason to regret that in this case it did happen. Our quarrel is not with what is being done. The minister has

made a good case for the necessity of taking action of the kind he has indicated. Our quarrel is with the way it was done and with the publicity that was attached to it and which brought into the matter the R.C.M.P. itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think in his closing remarks the Leader of the Opposition has expressed a proper concern for the position of the R.C.M.P. in connection with publicity of this kind. On that issue I am quite prepared to say there is a concern that it is wise and useful to discuss. What I objected to earlier was the form of appearing to suggest that the R.C.M.P. were volunteering statements and making announcements.
There are just one or two further impressions in this regard that it is still necessary to clear up before we deal with the issue itself of whether or not the police should answer questions of the press. The impression has been given-and I think I can readily understand how it might have been received-by the Leader of the Opposition, that the commissioner held a number of press meetings, held a press conference or gave a series of answers to questions by the press over a considerable period. That is not the case. The commissioner did not hold a press conference at all, as a matter of fact. On the very day the search warrants were executed, quite contrary to what the Leader of the Opposition said, it became a sensational story. It became a sensational event with the executing of search warrants all across Canada. The commissioner's office was deluged with phone calls from the press and so were the local divisional offices, I am told.
The press knew about it. They regarded it as sensational, because an operation of this type had never taken place in Canada before. It was not sensational because of what the commissioner said but it was sensational because of what happened. The press knew there was a big story here, and that knowledge could not be kept from them. The commissioner of the police was then faced with this question. Here is a big sensational story; are we going to keep mum about it and not answer questions and therefore leave the whole thing to speculation, or will we answer questions where it is proper for us to do so on the basis of giving factual information?
The decision taken was that the latter course would be followed. I think, on balance, that was a proper decision. From hindsight one might now say it would have been safer to decide not to say anything. If anyone holds that view in this particular case he 79951-0-367J
Supply-Justice
certainly could make a strong argument that it would have been safer not to say anything, but I think the wise and proper decision at the time was that in view of the widespread interest in the story and the unusual nature of the circumstances the answers that could properly be given should be given.
When you analyse the answers you will find that they were not widespread or sensational in themselves. There were not a repeated number of interviews. The Leader of the Opposition has referred to a large number of articles. The hon. gentleman himself, if he stops to think about it, I believe will realize that this always happens when the Canadian Press gets a story that is of national interest. The story is repeated all across Canada in the first place and it is frequently picked up by other papers and rerun as much as several days later.
And elaborated upon, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, and elaborated upon, as the hon. gentleman just said. Therefore the story of one interview with the commissioner creates the impression that a tremendous number of interviews were held on separate occasions, which is not the case at all.
1 also want to say that there was only one television interview about which we have information, only one appearance on television by any officer of the R.C.M.P. It is therefore quite incorrect to leave the impression that there were widespread interviews on television and widespread appearances by R.C.M.P. officers.
The one television interview was held in Vancouver. In view of what has been said about it I feel I should put the interview on the record, because the impression has been created that the officer who appeared on that interview made sensational statements, gave answers and facts which were sensational, and in effect divulged information he should not have divulged.
I think when I read the interview with this officer hon. members can judge for themselves that great discretion and judgment were exercised and that he answered no questions that he should not have answered and gave no information that he should not have given. Perhaps I should not give the name of the officer so it will not appear on the record, although if anyone wants to inquire I have no objection to giving it personally. The interview in question and answer form was as follows:
Q. Can you give us some idea of the extent of the raid carried out here in British Columbia?
A. All of the searches we conducted were done in the greater Vancouver area and amounted to approximately fifteen business establishments and homes.
Q. Have any arrests been made?
A. No arrests.

May I just deal with two points raised by the minister in a serious way in replying to what I said. In so far as the reason for and the background of the somewhat sensational publicity that this matter has received are concerned, I still think that was due in large part to the statement made in what was called an interview- I do not know whether it was an interview or not-by the commissioner that "our evidence indicates the majority came in that way". He was there referring to the majority of Chinese immigrants in the last 10 years, which would make the figure of 11,000 a reasonable one. Once that figure was given out, how could publicity of this kind be avoided? Surely the minister would agree that it is unfortunate that this publicity should be attached to a statement, even an answer to a press inquiry, made by the commissioner.
I am not criticizing the commissioner. I know what newspapers can do to statements of this kind. I have some headlines for which the commissioner is not responsible; but once you get into this situation you may be asking for exaggeration and trouble. I think we can preserve the R.C.M.P. from that kind of thing. It would perhaps be better for everybody, including the force, that when statements of this kind are made- the press has the right to information-they should be made by representatives of the government and not by the police.

So far as the broadcast is concerned, I do not want to give the impression that there was a lot on television. I saw one broadcast. It was a national program; therefore it went across the country. I do not take issue with what the officer of the R.C.M.P. said on this occasion. But it seems to me that when an investigation of this seriousness is being made, when we are in the middle of that investigation it might have been desirable to keep an R.C.M.P. officer off the screen and from talking about the investigation which was being conducted. However responsibly he may have discussed it right after he finished speaking there was a spokesman for the Chinese community who took issue with the R.C.M.P. in this matter. That, I think, was undesirable in the circumstances. This is the only point I am trying to make, Mr. Chairman; I think it is a valid one.

The Leader of the Opposition is, of course, making a great to-do about implied statements. I think this is shameful when you consider the fact that in Canada we have one of the finest forces of its kind in the world. Every hon. member has a duty to uphold its reputation.
He said it to protect it.
He continues to imply that that these statements have been made.

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, I am implying nothing. I have read quotations from newspapers attributed to the police which have not been denied by the minister. Perhaps the hon. member should not be too excited about it.
Of course the Leader of the Opposition believes everything that appears in the press, but he never inquires into the background.

I did not want to get involved in this controversy between the hon. member for Wetaskiwin and the Leader of the Opposition, but it does seem that every time the hon. member speaks in this house he starts out by using the word "shameful".
I have had a lot of lessons from you.
A few moments ago the minister said that a substantial number of Chinese Canadians are involved in this thing one way or another. Will the minister tell us what he meant by "substantial"?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think the words speak for themselves. I am not going to give a figure because we have not got all the evidence gathered and analysed yet. For just that reason the commissioner did not give a figure,
Supply-Justice
though he was asked about a figure. Incidentally, my clear recollection and knowledge is that figures of this order were being talked about openly. The press certainly were using this figure of 11,000 in their conversation before the warrants were executed on May 24; indeed ever since the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration made her announcement in January, very substantial figures of this order were being talked about, and it was in that context that one of the press men asked the commissioner, "Is it as high as 11,000?" And he said, "That is not my figure, but I would not quarrel with it". It was a figure commonly being mentioned.
With respect to the actual question asked, as to what I meant when I said "substantial numbers are involved in this in one way or another", I think these words have a perfectly clear meaning and I am not going to give a figure. We cannot give a figure. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration refused to give a figure. We will not be in a position to give figures until we have all the information before us.

I thought what the minister meant by "substantial" was what is meant by the use of the word under the Combines Investigation Act, but that is another matter.
I should like to deal briefly with the questionnaire. My complaint here is not that a questionnaire was necessary as a guide to the R.C.M. Police in eliciting information, so that when they got the information they would use the same questions all across the country and compile the results afterwards and come up with something worth while. I think it is necessary that such a method be used, but the difficulty which resulted in Prince Rupert- and I think the R.C.M. Police prejudiced themselves rather than anybody else prejudicing them-arose from the fact that an individual did in fact sign a piece of paper on which this information was contained.
People of Chinese extraction, especially those who have not been here too long, have certain attitudes. They group themselves together, as other people would do in a strange country, and are reluctant to append their signatures to anything. To their way of thinking a document is an official piece of paper and if they put their name or anybody else's name on it, it means that they are signing something official. In addition, a number of these people were asked to go down to the police station to answer questions. This indicated to them that some kind of full-fledged inquiry was being conducted and that these individual Chinese persons had to give the information requested. They thought they were obliged and forced to answer some of the questions when in fact that was not the case. They are not obliged to answer any

Supply-Justice
questions whatsoever, although if proceedings were taken under section 11 of the Immigration Act there would be some obligation on the part of the individual to answer those questions. The manner in which the questionnaire was used, the attitude or the approach of the R.C.M. Police, in fact almost forcing people to come down to the police station and requiring one person to sign such a document, prejudiced the R.C.M. Police.
In the back of the minds of the people of Prince Rupert still lurks another matter. Those who recall the attitude of a number of people in Prince Rupert toward the R.C.M. Police will recollect that two or three times over the past few years there have been some difficulties between the police and the people of Prince Rupert. The R.C.M. Police have been involved in skirmishes, antagonisms and things of that nature. Knowledge of this background is still there; it has not been overcome. On top of that undercurrent which still exists in the minds of some people there is the use of this questionnaire and the manner in which it stirred up those antagonisms which would be there naturally anyway. In this instance I think the R.C.M.P. did more damage to themselves in attempting to elicit this information than anybody else could possibly do.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, while what the hon. member has said has been expressed calmly I think it could perhaps create misunderstanding and an unfortunate impression if we do not get the matter into perspective again. It is true that there was a misuse of the questionnaire in this one case. That was a mistake. It has been rectified, and it has been made clear that the questionnaire was not for that purpose. That was a mistake which was quite easy to make, but it has been corrected.
With regard to the larger issue of whether the police should invite people to come to headquarters for questioning and interviewing, or whether there is anything here which is in any way suggestive of strong arm tactics, let us just consider the position for a moment. These interviews are necessarily lengthy. All the questions have to be translated through an interpreter and the answers have to be translated and written down. My hon. friend knows the Chinese people and knows that these interviews take a long time.
Are the police to go to a Chinese person and stand in the middle of his restaurant or laundry for two hours interviewing him with an interpreter present? That would be an imposition on the individual concerned. Similarly, should the person concerned have two large police officers in the front room of his home while an interview is conducted? No;

the normal, courteous and sensible thing to do is to say, "Will you please come down to headquarters? We would like to interview you and ask you some questions." For this to be represented as something which either strikes fear into the heart of the Chinese or is used to compel him to come to headquarters and thus create a bad impression in connection with the way the police are operating just does not seem to be reasonable when you think of what the alternative would be. The alternative would be for the interview to take place in the man's restaurant or store over a period of two hours with the public hearing all the questions and answers, or else to impose on the man in his home for the same length of time. I am quite sure that when people stop to think about the matter they will see the operation in its proper perspective, and will appreciate that these normal police operations have good reasons behind them and in many cases are based on what is, frankly, consideration for the public when you stop to analyse the matter.
Mr. Chairman-

I should like to reply to the minister's comments, and I express my appreciation to the hon. member for allowing me to do so. I do not think the Minister of Justice succeeded in getting the matter into perspective but rather succeeded in distorting it. Here are the circumstances that existed in the Chinese communities. There had been a statement that 11,000 of them had entered the country illegally, and whether or not that was an official announcement does not matter. The Chinese people had that understanding. In addition, search warrants were executed in a number of places across Canada just prior to the time the matter of the questionnaire was involved. Many people in the Chinese communities, in Prince Rupert for example, thought they were directly or indirectly involved. I do not know actually what they were thinking. However, with this background they are asked to go to R.C.M.P. headquarters and answer questions, and one of their number has to sign a document. As a result they immediately become concerned.
I think that puts the matter in its proper perspective. That is the way the Chinese people look at it, and that is why they have rebelled and held meetings to discuss the matter. That is why they went to a lawyer and were advised that they did not have to answer any of these questions. Looking at the matter from the point of view of the people in the Chinese communities, I think this is what their reaction would be and why they would think they were being subjected

to some sort of persecution in being asked to answer questions in the light of the other developments that had taken place just two or three weeks before.

Mr. Chairman, as an ex-member of the mounted police I think I can speak with some authority on one or two of these questions. First of all, the trouble involving the Chinese is a question of public relations, as everybody can readily understand. I think a great deal of to-do is being made about something which is quite simple. The R.C.M.P. are charged with maintaining security in Canada. It is not an easy job but rather one of the most difficult jobs in the world, because on occasion they must interfere or appear to interfere in people's private affairs. I cannot see how any well-adjusted citizens of Canada, whether they have been here all their lives or have only been here for a few days, can object to the honest attempts of the R.C.M.P. to keep our country secure.
I think it is more than wrong to drag in racial prejudices at a time like this. There are a great many Chinese in Canada who are very proud of their Canadian citizenship and are just as anxious as we are that people do not enter Canada from China or anywhere else against the laws of our country. Looking at the matter from the point of view of a Canadian citizen, it would seem that a few groups have chosen to make a great to-do about it, perhaps because they are guilty, perhaps because they have had some hand in the matter, perhaps because they are related to some of the people who are guilty, or perhaps for purely partisan political purposes, and have exaggerated and expanded one or two minor incidents to make them look like national scandals.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police are the finest police force in the world. They have operated now for a great many years, and I cannot imagine any force which operates with greater impartiality. Again I speak with some authority, because on two occasions I was relieved of my duties in the mounted police as a result of the strict observance of the regulations, once for having married without permission and again for indicating that I took an active interest in public affairs. For this I hold absolutely no rancour. I admire the mounted police for upholding the regulations in my case in the same way as they do with respect to every member of the force.
With respect to the question of public relations I should like to make this plea, and ask that it be given consideration by the commissioner and the department. I suggest that renewed attention should be given to what
Supply-Justice
we used to call the youth and police program. When this program was in operation I think the mounted police made more progress so far as good public relations are concerned, particularly among young people. We were instrumental in instituting safety patrols for school children throughout the length and breadth of this country. Young mounted policemen started baseball, football and swimming activities and judo and boxing classes. Wherever the program was put into effect so-called juvenile delinquency, which is just another way of saying that boys are having a good time, decreased. The boys started to play baseball and get themselves in shape. They began to take an interest in the Boy Scouts and to box, swim, fish, hunt and do all the things a boy would rather do than steal or break windows or get into other trouble.
Wherever you find one of these fine young mounted policemen, a grown up Boy Scout if you like, working among young people you will find that the record speaks for itself. These activities are not confined solely, of course, to the mounted police. Municipal and provincial police forces have also done signal work along the same lines, but the mounties have always taken the lead in these affairs. Again I would plead with the commissioner and the department to provide whatever funds are necessary to make police transport and sports equipment available, and to give full recognition to this work which is often done beyond the call of duty.
Recently the marriage regulations were improved. When I joined the mounted police in 1935 it was necessary for a recruit, no matter what his age, to wait six years before he could marry the girl of his choice. In 1937, without any consultation with those who had signed on the force, this regulation was changed to seven years. Some of us got a little desperate because we thought it might be changed to 12 years, so we went out and got married. At one time I believe half the members of the mounted police force were married without permission, and if it had not been for the war coming along and the fact that I volunteered for the provost corps, I might have got away with it, like many others including officers. However, when it was brought to the attention of my superiors I was treated in the impartial manner in which everybody else was treated, and relieved of my duties. This enabled me to go overseas with the other volunteers with whom I chummed. When I came back to this country I was forgiven and rehired.
I should like to say something about the question of pay. When my father was a mounted policeman he rode across the plains for 50 cents a day. However, at that time

Supply-Justice
50 cents would almost buy a quart of whisky, so the pay figured that way was not too much out of line with what it has been recently. Today, however, the job of a mounted policeman is very complicated. The standards are just as high, and they were always very high. We demand young men capable of holding down territories which are sometimes as large as some countries in Europe. I have patrolled a territory consisting of 14,000 square miles and supervised six other young men and their many duties. I feel that command pay is out of line these days. When a man has this responsibility I think he should be paid accordingly. I trust that the pay of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is about to be raised, and I hope substantially.
We have the finest police force in the world. I believe the people of Canada appreciate the service they are getting, and that they intend to pay these men according to the service rendered. It is true that in times past the men have been willing to work for next to nothing, but those days are gone forever. The public servant who is doing a good job today is entitled to a realistic rate of pay.
In so far as training is concerned, I think that would bear some looking into. I am quite in agreement with putting the young man on a horse, introducing him to that noble animal and getting him away from his mother. However, I feel that perhaps better training on a typewriter and in office procedure might be in order. Perhaps most people are not aware of the fact that the average mounted policeman spends as much time pounding a typewriter as he does in the field. We have not yet reached the stage where we believe there should be stenographers in every police detachment, so these young men have to type voluminous reports on every conceivable subject. I feel that more attention to business training would be very helpful in this paper age.
We are short of men in the mounted police today because it is a hard job requiring high standards, and the discipline is strict. I feel that if young men leaving school or university knew what a satisfying career it is, what fine training it is for public service and for public life, they would be glad to serve in the mounted police for 20 or 30 years. They would work with the finest young men in the country, and I think the job is second to none for excitement and for personal satisfaction. If I had to do it all over again I would be very pleased to do so.

All I can say is that I hope the pay will be brought up somewhere near the high standard of service which these young men give to this country.

Mr. Chairman, I shall be brief, but first of all I wish, on behalf of my constituents and many people in northern Canada, to express through the minister to the recently retired commanding officer of "G" division, Superintendent Henry Larsen, our thanks for his years of devotion and his many accomplishments. I need not recite to this committee the many accomplishments of this great man. I am sure that his name is in the hearts and minds of many Canadians, and his accomplishments are known not only in Canada but throughout many parts of the world. The sincerity and interest of Superintendent Larsen, not only in the enforcement of law but in the general welfare and social and economic conditions of the people of the north, are things he passed on to the many men who served under him. We in the north wish him many happy years in retirement.
We were happy also that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police appointed in his place a man with northern experience, Superintendent Fraser. I am sure that during the course of his northern service he has had the general welfare and condition of the people in that part of the country very much in mind. We are sure that in the future he will pass on these fine qualities to the men who succeed him.
This brings me to another point. I am wondering what the policy of the force is with regard to men who come out of the north. The other day, on July 1, I walked out of the house to take a look at the proceedings on the hill. I saw a man who had spent, to my knowledge, nine or ten years in northern Canada. I saw him standing there directing people, telling them where to stand. Is this all the force has for a man who has spent the better years of his life in the north? Is he to be brought here to direct traffic? Surely there must be some other position for a man with northern experience. Surely the force must have young recruits who could stand in front of this building as a decoration for the tourists, or walk around putting parking tickets on cars. I ask through you, Mr. Minister, that the commissioner look into this business of the transfer of personnel who return from northern Canada and who are trying to establish themselves in this so-called civilization we enjoy here.
I would also like to bring up another matter. I have heard rumours over the past year and a half that the R.C.M.P. in northern

Canada are going to be relegated to office boys. The reason I say this is that I understand the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources are considering putting men into many of the small, isolated communities in the north to take over responsibilities from the R.C.M.P. This all sounds very well, but at the same time in many of these places if the R.C.M.P. did not have to do a dog patrol to visit trappers' cabins or people on the trap lines they would have nothing to do. Their morale, as far as I am concerned, would go down to such an extent that you might as well have them out of the north altogether. Why have men sitting around in these communities doing nothing but pound a typewriter?
I say put the dog patrols back into these isolated places. In many of these isolated communities just the presence of an R.C.M.P. officer provides stability. I can tell you of many cases, in my own riding in particular, where in the past few years I have asked native people and others in these communities, "What do you think of the job which was originally done by the R.C.M.P. in game and forestry matters?" Of course a large part of our country has no forest, but we have forestry men running around the country looking after our forests. However, the inevitable answer I received was that the R.C.M.P. did a better job prior to these encroachments by northern affairs than has ever been done since.
I had occasion last year to ask natives in Fort Good Hope, "Who was the best public servant who ever spent any time in this community? Who did things because of his real interest in the people; interest in your housing and how you made out on the trap lines and your social and economic position?" The answer was a certain R.C.M.P. who had been stationed there some years before; I forget his name now. In any event this was how they felt.
Personally I feel that this co-ordinating committee which deals with northern Canada should be told that we do not need duplication of service in the north. The government should accept that. They are broke now trying to pay for what they have to pay for. Why duplicate the service in places like Fort Good Hope, Snowdrift, Resolution, Fort Providence and all those places? Give the R.C.M.P. man something to do. Give him the responsibility of visiting the trap lines, enforcing the game laws and doing the things he was trained to do.
Any R.C.M. Policeman who comes into that district can go into Fort Smith and, in co-operation with the game and forestry branch of the department of northern affairs,
Supply-Justice
take a course for a week or two and once a year be called back to discuss these matters with the officers of the department. To put a forestry man or a game man into an area where you have someone like the R.C.M.P. to look after that sort of thing costs a great deal of money. There is the salary of the man you send in, and his removal expenses from Ottawa. You have to construct a building for him to live in, which costs at least $25,000 to $30,000. You have to operate this establishment and put fuel oil into the tanks. You have to provide electricity. I say, why do we duplicate effort, particularly in these days when we are not that well off that we can throw money around hiring people to take over duties which would leave others with nothing to do.
I have heard a rumour that this coordinating committee is considering suggesting to the R.C.M.P. in my riding that their establishment in Fort Smith be enlarged They are going to provide Fort Smith with lots of aircraft and take all the R.C.M.P. out of Snowdrift or wherever they are in these isolated communities. Of course the R C M P will be left at places like Yellowknife and Hay river, where there is a fair population, but the rest will be put into Fort Smith.
Now, let us suppose that someone in Snowdrift shoots somebody else. Someone will say "We will send a wire to Fort Smith for the mounties". Of course weather conditions are never too good, so maybe the mountie will not get there for five days. In the meantime this man, who has probably gone berserk, has shot half the community. This is the way they want to save money; they would put them all into Fort Smith.
I say the only thing to do is to put the R.C.M.P. to work; put them to work which every young man would enjoy, such as following a dog team, visiting the trap lines, taking an interest in the community and in community housing for these native people. Young men who go north heard about those things when they joined the R.C.M.P. Half of them would never join if they thought they would go north to pound a typewriter filling out birth statistics and family allowance forms.
I hope the minister suggests to his colleague the minister of northern affairs that he consider that rather than putting more people into these areas, he put the R.C.M.P. back to work. If there is a case where a community requires an Indian agent or an assistant agent to do something for the natives, for example to fill out statistics and possibly lend a hand in community projects, then that is fine; put in an agent.
It appears that now we want to fill the country with welfare officers. I understand

Supply-Justice
that the civil service commission cannot hire a welfare officer unless he has a Ph.D. I have never heard of anything like it. The man has never seen an Eskimo, but he has to have a Ph.D. I know mounties and public servants who have been in the north and are still there who possibly had no more than a high school education, but they do have in their hearts a desire to do something for these people.
What happens today when they send in a welfare officer? Does he go to the R.C.M.P. and say, "What did you fellows do in these cases, because I want to try something"? Oh, no; to hell with the R.C.M.P. Does he go to the Hudson's Bay man who has spent 40 years in the north? Hell, no; not the Hudson's Bay man; he is stealing from the natives, piling fur and beaver skins up to the top of the barrel in order to buy a rifle. The days of the Hudson's Bay Company exploiting the Indians has gone, and have been gone for some years, but does he go to these men with experience? Heck, no. Does he go to any one of the missionaries, Anglican or Roman Catholic, and say, "What was your experience?" No. So they go ahead and do the same old thing that the missionaries tried, that the R.C.M.P. may have tried, or that the Hudson's Bay company may have tried, and all failed. But they are going to try it again.
I am tired of this same old rigmarole. I say, let us put the R.C.M.P. back to work. If you want to do something for the man who is slugging behind a dog team in those isolated communities, then do something like the department of northern affairs has done, or is still doing, and pay the teacher an extra $1,000 a year to do work other than he would normally do as a teacher; welfare work. At one time the R.C.M.P. were allowed to have trap lines to help them out, but that was taken away from them. Nowadays no one visits the isolated trappers. I hope the minister will consider these suggestions, and that he will not let this high-level interdepartmental committee force anything down his throat that he does no want to accept.
I say again that I deplore this tendency to take away certain duties from the R.C.M.P. in isolated communities and give them to other people who, it is claimed, are more qualified. This all stems from the starvation of Eskimos at Garry Lake a few years ago. We have read reports about this. Farley Mowat in his writings has blamed the R.C.M.P. for these deaths. This same Farley Mowat was given access to files in the department of northern affairs that I am not able to see, nor is any other member of this house

able to see them. But the policy of the department of northern affairs was, if we can't lick them let's join them.
That is a fine attitude. About that time in Maclean's magazine-it was January 31 of last year-a short article appeared under a headline "Background": "The Mounties' Rule in the North has been Challenged by the Federal Department of Northern Affairs". Let me say right away that the mounties did not rule in the north, anyhow; the mounties did a job in the north. The article went on to say:
The main issue; Eskimo policy. The resignation of Doug Wilkinson, best-known white man in the Arctic-
That is a real laugh.
-he's author of the award-winning "Land of the Long Day"-from northern affairs recently brought the conflict into the open. Wilkinson's gripe: Eskimos in some cases die of starvation.
This refers to Garry Lake, where this northern service officer was stationed as a welfare officer looking after the interests of those Eskimos, or I always thought the duties of a northern service officer were to look after the welfare of the Eskimos. Of course since that time I have not got out of that department an answer that suits me. I do not know what their duties are-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I think I should remind the hon. gentleman that these are the estimates of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I know he is trying to make a point, and I think the Chair has been lenient in allowing him to make his point of comparison, but I do wish he would come back now to the consideration of the R.C.M.P. and not the department of northern affairs.

Thank you. You have suggested, Mr. Chairman, that I have been trying to make a point. I want to impress this upon the commissioner of the R.C.M.P. or on whoever is going to sit on this interdepartmental committee. I am going to be very brief. Up to now, anyway, I have not been able to find out what are the duties of a northern service officer. In recent years many have been elevated to area administrators. People in the north wonder now whose duty it is to look after the welfare of Eskimos.
This article went on to say:
Northern affairs hasn't enough authority or facilities to help them, and it isn't the mounties' job. Although an officer of the government, Wilkinson had to buy his own plane to visit Eskimo settlements. Meanwhile, to police the north, mounties have every facility, including planes.
Mr. Wilkinson, or whoever wrote this article, does not know anything about what

the R.C.M.P. have done in the north if he thinks that all the R.C.M.P. have to do is police the north.
Mr. Chairman, on your suggestion I am going to end my remarks, but I hope the minister will consider some of the suggestions I have made, particularly as to the duties in the future of R.C.M.P. officers in the north. If there is any prospect of many of their duties being taken away from them, I personally feel that the R.C.M.P. will begin to acquire a very low opinion of the position they hold; because they will be relegated, as I say, to a strictly office type of job. The hon. member for Athabasca wants more typewriters. Well, let us keep the typewriter men down here; we do not want them in the north.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I rise only for one purpose, and that is with regard to the statement made by the hon. member for Mackenzie River that men are brought down from the north and then put on guard duty here on parliament hill with nothing better to do than direct the traffic or be a tourist attraction.
Unfortunately the hon. member did not identify the man he had in mind, as is perhaps right, but in consequence I have not had the opportunity to find out what the circumstances are. Now what will happen is, I suppose, that it will go on record and in the press that this is what the police are doing, but I know it is not what they are doing. Men are not brought down from the north to carry out traffic and guard duty on parliament hill.
July 1 was a special occasion. We have not many reserves, and it might well be that a man who was on some other duty altogether, having come out from the north, was brought up here on July 1 to help with the special problem of controlling the traffic and the crowd on that day; but for the hon. member to suggest that it would be our policy to bring men out of the north after years of service there and put them on parliament hill is absurd, and I am sure he knows it. It may have been done on that special day, but I think it is unfortunate that an impression to the effect that he was posted to parliament hill should be created. I feel bound to point out also that the hon. member could easily have checked on whether there was really cause for complaint before splashing it all over the record here on an inaccurate basis.
I do assure him and the committee that I know the feelings of the men who have served in the north. I went up there myself and spent two weeks in the western half of the Northwest Territories just to get some idea of what goes on. 1 know that the men up there have
Supply-Justice
a special pride in their status in the force and in their northern service, and many do not want to leave. But of course the opportunities for promotion are limited if they were to stay always in "G" division, which is one of the smaller divisions of the force, so they are posted out again. When they come out they are brought out on promotion and are given a different type of duty to perform so they may become more experienced policemen and have the opportunity of going right up through the force, which they would not have if they stayed in "G" division.
I know there is a problem in this respect. Many men who show great initiative in isolated northern posts are brought down and put perhaps on highway patrol somewhere in what they call the outside. Some people ask why should a man who has shown all this resourcefulness sustain this terrible comedown? Well, the fact is that highway patrol is a large part of a policeman's duty, and a large part of the duty of a police force. If a man is to have an opportunity for promotion he has to have experience in all parts of police work.
I can give the hon. member one example of a constable who came out after two years at Ellesmere island, and who is now in Ottawa. He was brought out for the purpose of being sent to university. Many of these northern men are men of great initiative, and we try to give them opportunities in the postings that are made after they come out from the north. I can assure the committee that no one who comes out from the north is posted to parliament hill.

I should like to clear up a
small misapprehension. 1 certainly did not wish to leave the impression that I think the mounted police should be relegated to a typewriter. What I was pleading for was a little more training on the typewriter. Due to the many technical jobs which a mountie is called upon to perform these days, proficiency on the typewriter is absolutely essential. I did not like the typewriter myself, and I do not think many of our boys do, but I spent many laborious hours searching for the keys with two fingers, and had I learned the touch system I would have been able to provide better reports more rapidly and thus devote more time to the more interesting aspects of police work.

Item agreed to.
375. Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and equipment, $3,804,029.

Mr. Chairman, some time ago I had occasion to discuss the new police building in the Sudbury area, of which the citizens of Sudbury and I am sure the police

Supply-Justice
officers as well are proud. There seems to be some difficulty in making arrangements for landscaping the grounds of this building. The choice of the site was proper. The building is located on the outskirts of Sudbury on a large piece of property. The building unfortunately appears rather low, but this is not too serious. However, when you drive past the place you cannot help but think it resembles a hydro substation, a warehouse, a garage for storing telephone trucks or some similar building. There are garage doors facing the street. In the interests of good public relations, and with a view to creating a good impression on those who visit the building, I think some improvement should be made in its appearance.
I am advised that some difficulty has been encountered in attempting to obtain the trees and shrubs required to beautify the building. Perhaps the minister would investigate the situation and assist in bringing about an improvement to this fine building.

Mr. Chairman, could the minister inform the committee whether the department intends to build adequate quarters for the R.C.M.P. detachment in the town of Shippegan in Gloucester county? This is an important detachment covering a large district, including the islands of Shippegan and Miscou. I believe they deserve better quarters.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have to advise the hon.
member that there is nothing in this year's estimates for Shippegan.

I urge the minister to have his department take this matter into consideration. I am familiar with the situation there. The accommodation provided is inadequate, and these men deserve better accommodation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I thank the hon. member for bringing this to our attention. It will be considered. We are faced with a big problem in building quarters. There are many centres where accommodation has been inadequate for some time. We have had to establish a system of priority, but we will have a look at Shippegan.

Nicholson, former commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, shall be paid, as of the day he ceased to be commissioner, a pension for life of one fiftieth of his pay at the time of his retirement for each completed year of service, $1.
