speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I thank the committee for its consideration.
DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE Customs and excise divisions-
258. General administration, $4,807,852.

Mr. Chairman, I trust the minister has an opening statement to make. Does he wish to segregate the discussion of the C.B.C. and the Department of National Revenue, or will both be discussable under this first item?

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the C.B.C. will be entirely separate from the Department of National Revenue. I propose to proceed, subject to the wish of the committee, with the customs and excise divisions, then with the taxation division of the Department of National Revenue, and following that with the C.B.C. and the board of broadcast governors.
I appreciate the fact that there may be some overlapping as between the C.B.C. and the board, and I do not think we should be too strict in attempting to hold the discussion to one element or the other. Of course if specific questions are asked about either the C.B.C. or the board I would ask that they be directed to me when the respective officers are before us.
I do not propose to make a lengthy statement on this question, but with respect to the customs and excise divisions perhaps I should say a word or two, because after all this is one branch of government without which it would be very difficult to carry on the government of Canada. As a matter of courtesy I perhaps should refer to the committee which met last year and interviewed the officers of the Department of National Revenue and particularly of the customs and excise division. They made three recommendations: one dealing with labelling of imported goods; one dealing with the tariff status of engineering drawings; and one dealing with imported articles exempt from sales and excise tax. Without boring or taking up the time of the committee I think I can say in brief that the department has tried to comply, and I believe has complied with the recommendations of the committee in so far as it was possible to do so. If there are any specific questions on that matter I should be glad to deal with them later on when we are dealing with the figures of the department.

I might point out in passing, Mr. Chairman, that the primary function of this division of the department, which is an administrative one, is the collecting of revenue. The total revenue collected by this division in the past fiscal year amounted to $2,152,553,299, which is an increase of 12.4 per cent over the revenue collected in the preceding year.
Our responsibility, of course, also extends to the administration of various acts and the inspection of vehicles coming across the border, and so on. There has been a substantial increase in the business in that direction. Vehicles reporting through customs last year totalled approximately 9 million, which was 190,000 more than the previous year.
This is a matter which I should like to draw to the attention of the committee with humility but also with a little bit of pride, I think. Despite all this increase in activity we have managed to reduce our total estimates by $608,000 as compared with last year. When you consider, that salaries alone amount to over 91 per cent of our total estimates I think you will agree that this is indicative of a very healthy appreciation on the part of the administration of this division of the virtues of efficiency and economy. For this I take no credit to myself at all except for responsibility for the division, but I do want to pay a well-deserved tribute to the officers of the division who have been able to achieve this economy and at the same time do more work than has been done heretofore.
It is within this area of estimated expenditure for salaries that we have been able to make a substantial reduction. We have reduced the number of establishments in the department by 99 and I might say that the dilution has not resulted in people being fired from the department. We have transferred them from one branch to another. It has been accomplished by bringing in more efficient methods, by the introduction to some extent of machines, computing devices and so on. In any event, we have achieved that. When we come to taxation I can point out that the same comparable result has been achieved there, and I think this is the one department of government which two years in succession has reported a decrease in expenditures and an increase in the work load which has been I believe satisfactorily carried out by the department.
Various changes have been made in the administrative branch during the year. I might refer to one or two of them in passing. Beginning with those which we have made to try to make it more convenient for the public as well as for efficiency for ourselves has been the abolition during the year of the customs form E-60, which Canadians, as many
Supply-National Revenue of you will recall, had to complete in respect of their motor vehicles when leaving Canada. We have made a change there and, judging from the reaction of the public, this change has been very well received.
Another change of notable effectiveness was the revising of the traveler's vehicle permit which has had the effect of considerably speeding up the clearance through customs of foreign travelers entering our country.
Then there is the new procedure with respect to the reporting of aircraft used for health or pleasure purposes and which are not carrying goods. Under this new system Canadians can proceed directly to a foreign country without first reporting to customs, and on returning to Canada complete at one time the outward and the inward reports.
I could draw the attention of the committee to various matters such as these which the division has brought into effect during the last year and which I think have resulted in not only increased efficiency but also better service in so far as the public is concerned. However, I do not intend to take up the time of the committee in dealing further with these general matters, but I shall be very glad to attempt to answer any specific questions and also reply to any comments which may be made during the course of this discussion.
I understand that two separate discussions will take place, one on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the other on the Department of National Revenue?
That is right.

And that the subheadings of the Department of National Revenue will be discussed on item 1. We all appreciate the fact that we are now discussing the department which collects revenue for the government of Canada. On other occasions we have been dealing with departments which spend the money which the Minister of National Revenue collects.
The minister mentioned that there has been a small decrease in the cost of the operations and in the estimates of this department. We have been told that certain devices have been installed in the department and we also realize that possibly some other changes may be made. The minister has indicated to the committee that some changes have been made by shifting operations from one section of the country to another. This shifting of operations may create not necessarily grave embarrassment but certain difficulties. I should like to ask the minister some questions with respect to the northern Ontario office which is located in the new federal building at Sudbury. Apparently in the last year or so directions have gone out that what are known as

Supply-National Revenue short forms for taxation purposes should be sent directly to Ottawa and not go through the Sudbury office as was the custom in years gone by.
May I interrupt the hon. member. I think he is referring to the income tax office and not the customs office. I would prefer to have that matter raised when we are dealing with taxation.
I thought we were dealing with the item.

We can deal with the item if the hon. member wishes, but as far as answering specific questions is concerned, I would not want to take the responsibility for answering questions with respect to taxation without the taxing officers present.

My remarks are of a general nature and have to do with the remarks the minister made. We find that directions have been given to the effect that the short forms should be sent directly to Ottawa. Can the minister tell me whether this means that there will be certain changes made in the Sudbury office and that possibly the work that is now done in that office will be done by people or machinery in the Ottawa office? Will the staff in the Sudbury office, which is the main office for northern Ontario, be reduced? As I understand it, the forms for as far away as Sault Ste. Marie were handled in the Sudbury office. People have been made aware of the fact that a request has been made for the short forms to be sent directly to Ottawa. Does this mean that there will be a curtailment of staff in the Sudbury area and an appreciable increase of staff in the Ottawa office? Were the facilities in Sudbury not capable of taking care of the northern Ontario forms?
I will deal with that, Mr. Chairman, when we come to item 262.

At the
outset of my remarks I should like to congratulate the Minister of National Revenue on the wonderful job he has done in his department. I remember that when the estimates of his department were before the committee on estimates of the House of Commons we were very impressed with the way in which he ran his department. I should also like to take this opportunity to congratulate the hon. member for Edmonton West on his appointment as parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Revenue.
I come from a riding which is completely industrial and urban. It is a riding that depends upon imports and exports, on manufacturing and on the protection of manufacturing in this country. I have heard it said


from time to time that our opponents on the other side of the house are the great free traders. I found it very interesting to sit in the house and hear the hon. member for Essex East talk about protection for the automotive industry. It did my heart good to find that the great Liberal free traders have finally come to the realization that, with an economy such as we have today, with a country of 17 million people compared with 180 million people in the United States and so many millions in Europe awakening from the second world war, the impact of imported manufactured products is being felt by Canadian manufacturers.
I also realize that the import and export position of the country is not a matter that comes primarily within the jurisdiction of the Minister of National Revenue although I know that in the past several months the mayors and reeves of the country, the labour unions, the automotive industry and the chamber of commerce have been knocking on the door of the genial minister. I might also point out that the problem of imports into our country today is basically caused by exports into our country from the nation to the south of us. We hear a great deal about the low cost labour content areas of the world such as Japan and certain parts of Europe but my prime consideration today is the United States of America. I am not speaking as an anti-American because I have many good friends there. I am talking as a proCanadian vitally interested in my community and in looking after the interests of the workers in the riding of Hamilton South.
I should like to talk about the cotton textile industry purely as an example. Some people may say that this is a bad industry to take as an example because of its very desperate position in the country today but from reading the newspapers and the briefs of the mayors and reeves, of the textile industry and of the automotive industry apparently there are many interests that are looking for action on the part of the government to help them in their plight. I know that the industrialists and the labour unions have a very definite responsibility in this connection and I know that they cannot make up their minds what to do. However, purely by way of example, I should like to talk about the cotton industry in Canada today as it is affected by the Customs Tariff.
It is my understanding that before 1953 the cotton industry experienced relatively good times in Canada because it had its own markets and the awakening of Europe had not taken place. The United States were recovering from the effects of the war and were looking after their own domestic market. In

1956, for example, the cotton manufacturing industry in Canada had some 22,500 employees. 1 note with some distress, and again I am not trying to be political about the matter, that at the end of 1959 there were only 16,000 employees in that industry, a drop of 6,000.
It seems to me that with regard to any problem there must be symptoms of the disease, the disease itself and there must be solutions. I have heard it said by many members as well as some members of the other place that the textile industry did not look after its own interests, that it did not increase production and buy new machinery. This may be all very well but the remarks I intend to make today have to do with a matter under the direct responsibility of the Minister of National Revenue.
I understand that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is concerned with export markets and achieving a good balance of trade but in directing these remarks to the Minister of National Revenue now I have the specific point in mind that governments have a definite responsibility with respect to secondary manufacturing in Canada. I am not one of those who believe in complete government interference because I am a Conservative but I believe that where government interference is needed it should be exerted with all force.
Section 6A of the Customs Tariff was introduced by the former government in 1955 but they did not take any action under it. The section provided that where subsidized goods are imported into Canada directly or indirectly from a foreign country the Minister of National Revenue may take action when Canadian industries are being hurt. Section 6A of the Customs Tariff reads in part as follows:
6A. (1) Where in the opinion of the governor in council subsidized goods of a class or kind made or produced in Canada have been or may be directly or indirectly imported into Canada, he may declare such goods to be subject to an additional duty on their importation equal to the amount of the subsidy on those goods as determined by him.
As far as the cotton industry in concerned, in 1956 the United States congress passed an act which provided, with respect to manufactured cotton goods exported from the United States, no matter to which country they went, for the payment of a subsidy on such exports equivalent in some instances to five cents a pound and in some instances as high as 17 cents a pound, representing about seven or eight cents on the dollar. Ironically this legislation came into effect in the spring of 1956 when there were 22,500 people employed in the Canadian cotton industry. In
Supply-National Revenue the past the former government used to talk about its vigorous policy with respect to the United States, but I cannot seem to recall Canadian representatives going to the United States at that time and telling these people that they could not do this to Canada, that we on the North American continent are in the same economic climate, that we have the same wage scales and therefore they could not apply a subsidy on exports from their country into Canada because it would hurt the Canadian cotton industry and at the same time other such subsidies would hurt other industries. I do not recall them ever doing this.
The position is that on cotton goods exported from the United States to all countries the United States have paid subsidies amounting to some $54 million since 1956 and on exports to Canada they have paid subsidies amounting to over $13 million. I know the minister may say to me that there must be proof that the United States are violating the section of the Customs Tariff, that they are not playing the game with us, that they are not going along with the general agreement of tariffs and trade under which the countries concerned are supposed to play fair with each other.
Again as a pro-Canadian and not an antiAmerican I say that businessmen in the cotton textile industries of the United States have used the section in the Customs Tariff to further their own ends with the result that 6,000 people have been put out of work, some 400 to 500 in my own district. I have a letter here written by a United States manufacturer of cotton goods to a Canadian importer in Toronto, Ontario. The letter points out how advantage can be taken of a loophole in section 6A of the Customs Tariff. The first paragraph of the letter indicates the price of the cotton material in question and the second paragraph reads as follows:
In addition, we will allow, to an associate or affiliate of yours in the United States, a rebate of $.07 per net pound. We will show on the customs invoice that we are allowing such a rebate to the firm you designate-
In the broad sense the Minister of National Revenue has no responsibility to take action by the imposition of a dumping duty because there is no indication on the invoice that this is being done. However, I also understand that investigators from the Department of National Revenue can go to the United States, call upon manufacturers and say that in the interests of good relationships they would like to see how they are running their businesses. This letter states that an amount of seven cents per pound will be paid. A manufacturer in my own riding tried this. He bought so many thousand yards of cotton goods in the United States

Supply-National Revenue and there was deposited in a British bank an amount equal to $2,200, which did not appear on the customs invoice.
The cotton industry is an example of one of these producers who is having a tough enough time competing with the Japanese in the world market without some smart businessmen in the United States taking advantage of the situation. Let us not fool anyone. Imports of United States cotton manufactured goods, with the same labour content as our cotton goods, have come into this country in quite substantial amounts during the last three years. It seems to me that these imports are coming into the country because these people are taking advantage of this United States legislation to hurt Canadian manufacturers. If there were free competition both ways across the border I would be all for letting everyone find his own level. However, when a foreign government enacts legislation subsidizing the exports of a specific industry, the products of which are manufactured in Canada, then I think the Minister of National Revenue and his learned officials should look into all the ramifications of the situation.
I believe if they did that they would draw the conclusion that two things would have to be done. Either the officials of the Department of National Revenue or the Department of Finance would have to go down to the United States and request them to discontinue paying a subsidy on these goods coming into Canada or we must take the bull by the horns and invoke this section 6A of the tariff act by order in council. Then the United States manufacturers who are shipping millions of dollars worth of cotton goods into Canada by depositing moneys outside the country for the benefit of the Canadian importers-not the manufacturers but the fellows sitting along St. Lawrence street in Montreal-would be prevented from doing so. In the last two or three years many people in my riding have been put out of work as a result of this practice. It is the responsibility of this government, therefore, to have a close look at section 6A of the Customs Tariff or alternatively to ask the United States to quit paying the subsidy on goods coming into Canada.
As a result of conversations I have had with people in the United States I do not believe it would be possible for the United States to discontinue paying the subsidy because their legislation says they must pay an export subsidy on cotton goods which go out of the United States. The only alternative this government has then is for the Department of National Revenue to invoke section 6A of the Customs Tariff. This would be of benefit to the Canadian textile manufacturers. I have talked to some 50 or 60 people in the

past few months and they are convinced that this would help a great deal.
Before I resume my seat, I should like to state again that I am sure each one of us has problems in our constituency and unless we get up and put them forward the minister will not find out about them. I am sure he is aware of this problem, however. I feel so strongly about it that I thought today I might use part of my time by speaking about this industry. However, this is not the only industry in which we have this situation. There is the woodworking industry and other secondary industries in my riding that are feeling the result of the price squeeze from competition from products from Europe and Japan which have this low labour content. I have been told that within the last few months the Steel Company of Canada has not sold a keg of nails west of Winnipeg. This worries me. I suppose the Minister of National Revenue has enough worries at the present time, but I do ask him to take a look at this special problem to which I have referred. I hope he will take this under advisement and give adequate consideration to it.

Mr. Chairman, being located along the Canada-United States boundary, the constituency of Brome-Missisquoi has a number of offices coming under the responsibility of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan). I should therefore like to discuss briefly the estimates of his department.
First of all, may I take this opportunity to commend the officials for the way the offices are operated and kept up. The people of Brome-Missisquoi have noted a number of improvements in those offices.
On behalf of the people of the Abercorn district, I wish to thank the minister and the officials of his department for providing that district with a new building, an exceptionally fine structure.
Mr. Chairman, I realize that most public buildings in Phillipsburg, come under the Department of Public Works. However I should like to refer very briefly to the fact that the department is planning to build a new warehouse in Phillipsburg and that, for various reasons unknown to me, there have been delays in the planning stage. I hope the plans will soon be ready, so that construction of this building in Phillipsburg may be completed as soon as possible.
(Text):
I should like to state briefly, Mr. Chairman, that Brome-Missisquoi is situated along the

border of the United States, mostly along the border of Vermont. I have had occasion to visit all the customs and immigration offices in my district over the past year. I should like to mention the fact that the officers at these border points are known to have treated the public, and are still treating the public, in a most courteous manner. I have said this before when these estimates were before the estimates committee, but I should like to repeat it. I feel that the officers of the departments of customs and immigration, perhaps more than any other officers, are the good will ambassadors of the people of Canada. I am very proud of the men who serve the department in my particular district. Every day they are dealing with visitors from the United States, ft is very important that this high degree of courtesy exhibited by these officers be underlined. I should like to congratulate the minister for encouraging this situation, and I know it will be emphasized in the future.
In talking with the various officers in my riding whom I visited, the question of pay often came up. I am sure the civil service authorities and the officers in the minister's department will give these demands most serious consideration.
I am going to deal for a moment, very briefly, with a general subject which has been touched upon already by the speaker who preceded me, and that is the question of dumping. I do not want to go into it in detail today, but the hon. member who preceded me said it not only affected the textile industry in his riding but affected many other products. The same is true of my riding, which is an eastern Canadian riding. The textile industry has in the past been seriously affected by dumping. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate teased me in this connection by saying that the question of dumping was a tariff question. Such is not the case. The question of dumping today, and I think this should be underlined and brought to the attention of the public, does not in any way relate to a classical discussion of high or low tariffs. It is an entirely separate question. Those who suggest we should discuss the problem and confuse it with tariff questions are doing a disservice to the country.
The same could be true of a quota system. These questions are perhaps related but they should be discussed separately from the dumping problem per se. I should like to congratulate the minister upon the fact that special officers were appointed and duly trained in the past in order to enforce dumping procedures. I know that the department, certainly at the top echelon, is most seriously
Supply-National Revenue aware of the problem of dumping goods produced in the United States on the Canadian market. I should like to feel certain that these procedures are being vigorously and rigorously enforced all down the line.
In a day and age where we must recognize the fact that trade must expand, with the interdependence of nations in an expanding world economy, we must underline the benefits of expanding many aspects of free trade. Yet the dumping question is a serious one. It is brought to my attention almost every week by various people and companies in my constituency. I know the minister has taken vigorous steps in his department to train officers at the local level to enforce our dumping procedures. Like the previous speaker, I would say in my area not only is the textile industry affected but other industries too.
So, in summing up I should like to thank the minister for the great improvements which are being made in my riding in the accommodations sections of buildings. I would also like to congratulate him for the courteous treatment customs officers are affording to the public, be they Canadians or visitors. In any event they are good will ambassadors for our people and for our country. I would also underline the fact that dumping procedures should be rigorously enforced right down the line to the local level and perhaps the minister will report whether an advance is being made in this direction.

There are a couple of minor points I want to ask about and the initial one has to do with the role that his department plays as a sort of censor of obscene literature. The minister will prehaps remember that I was quite frightened and still am by the legislation introduced last year by the Minister of Justice which amended the Criminal Code. As I contended at that time, this legislation put into the hands of magistrates and provincial attorneys general power which would seem to be power to act as censors for the whole country. We have recently had a case where a Montreal judge ruled against the book "Lady Chat-terley's Lover" by D. H. Lawrence, and I have not been able to find out whether any instructions have gone forward through the provincial attorney general's office in Quebec across the country as a result of that decision.
I have seen it stated in a number of press reports now that "Lady Chatterley's Lover" has been banned from sale in Canada, and I should like to know whether any instructions have gone forward to the minister's officials to bar the entry of that publication

Supply-National Revenue into Canada. I know that most of the copies available for sale in Canada must have come through the customs office.
I should like to know what effect the new legislation has had upon the approach of the minister's officials in examining literature coming into this country. I should like to know how many books the minister himself in the past year has ruled to be unfit after examination, and whether he is in a position to tell me, perhaps not in the committee but privately as a result of a question placed on the order paper, just what these particular books are.
I should also like a statement from him as to how he is facing up to a problem mentioned before with regard to obscene publications and obscenity in the form of records, tapes and that sort of thing.
I would especially like an assurance from the minister that his officials are being as liberal as he gave us to believe in the past they would be in their interpretations. I know from my own examination of material in New York and Paris, there are certain kinds of literature that we do not need in this country. At the same time one cannot help but be a little frightened by the censors. I am especially frightened by the ruling of the Montreal magistrate, because if we have any Canadian literary men of merit it seems to me that the two representatives who have spoken in favour of this particular book were such. Yet their particular views and advice was ignored by the magistrate, and he said in effect that what they said about it was merely their own opinions. What else do you have in censorship matters but opinions and judgments? Quite frankly I tell the minister that I have a little more faith in some of the customs officials than I have in some of the magistrates in this country.
The other matter is more specific and relates to an answer I got to a question concerning ports and revenue stations which are not on or immediately adjacent to the international boundary or are on the Atlantic or Pacific coasts, and the costs of maintaining these particular ports and their revenues. My question was that I wanted an indication of the ports with revenue of less than $60,000 a year and I have been given a list which gives me 13 of these ports. I have just checked through them and I discover there is one in Southampton, Ontario, for which the total operation costs for 1959 and 1960 are set out, amounting to $4,812. By checking the annual report I see that the year before the total revenue for this particular port was in the neighbourhood of $7,800. I checked Drumheller in Alberta and I found

that the expenses are about $4,400 and the total revenue last year was around $8,000. For Southampton, Ontario the expenditures are about $5,000 and the total revenue about $18,000.
I am interested in this because I hear the argument that we have a number of ports and outports which are completely unnecessary in terms of the volume of business they do. This has been triggered by the changing situation which has taken place at the Fort William customs office in the past year or so, to which I made no objection; but it seems to me the minister or his deputy minister might well look at these ports which have such low revenue and this rather constant expense. It certainly seems to me we should have more consolidation in this field.
I admit I cannot carry this argument too far from the statistics that have been filed, but if you have a place which costs $5,000 and produces an income of just over $7,000 a year, then I begin to wonder whether the service could not be transferred to another place.
I would not like to sit down without making reference to the few occasions upon which I have had to deal with the department through the deputy minister. I have heard him referred to as the oldest of the old Ottawa warhorses, and of course in the nicest way possible so far as the use of that term is concerned. I have always found him very pleasant to deal with.
The last question I want to ask the minister again requires detail which he may have. I should like to know how many special cases under section 38 of the Customs Act have been determined in the last year by the minister. I should also like to know the nature of the goods involved and the country of their origin.
I hope to have some more remarks tc make later on when we are dealing with the taxation division and also with regard to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
A number of hon. members mentioned that the customs people at the border points have always been fair, and I should like to say that that has also been my experience.
I should also like to ask the minister for some petty detail. We are trying to have an extension of our ski facilities at the lake-head and we would like an assurance that next winter, when we will have a plane bringing up 3,000 skiers from Minneapolis on the week ends, that the unofficial arrangement which was made last winter as a result of our request will continue and that there will be no worries on that score.

I should like to compliment the minister on what he has described as the economy made in his department. I see that

expenditure is down this year, as it was last year, and I can only hope that this process continues through other departments of government, because if it does the hon. gentleman will have less to collect in his own department.
The minister referred to the movement of traffic across the international boundary, and I can say that at Niagara Falls and Fort Erie, places with which I am familiar, the movement of traffic over those crossings has been facilitated by action taken by the department. I should like to pay tribute to the officers at the bridges, the customs officers as well as those in the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
I heard three hon. members here talking about dumping. I should like to ask the minister how many cases members of his staff have investigated, how many investigations have been made in the United States and what action has been taken as far as the customs tariff in concerned.
One question that I wish to raise has to do with the Canadian duty-free shops, and I think this matter could be discussed now, inasmuch as these shops, or the goods sold by them would be duty free and free of sales tax. I heard some time ago, and I have seen it in the press on several occasions, that one such shop was to be opened in the neighbourhood of the Canadian end of the Ivy Lea bridge, one or two in British Columbia and, one I think, at Niagara Falls. I do not know whether there are to be any others or not. These duty-free shops will probably sell luxury goods which would be admitted into Canada free of duty, free of Canadian sales tax and free of excise tax. They would include such articles as women's purses, perfumes, handbags and other luxury items. I know that the retail merchants association came here to make representations to the Prime Minister and, I think, to other members of the cabinet against the opening of the shops, and I think that in cases where local stores are selling similar articles the establishment of these shops might well interfere with their sales. I should like to hear from the minister on this point.
I can remember being down south, and about the only thing sold in these stores in Jamaica seemed to be large bottles of Scotch whisky, and rum. However, I think the merchants should be given every consideration, and I know that the merchants in Niagara Falls are greatly concerned over this matter, because citizens of the United States coming into Canada who are outside that country for 48 hours can take back $200 worth of goods with them free of duty. They can do that once a month, and if they buy certain of these luxury articles in duty-free
Supply-National Revenue shops that is likely to cut down the purchases they might otherwise make elsewhere in legitimate stores. I should like to hear from the minister on that point.

Since the minister wishes that we should discuss customs duty provisions at this time I should like to direct his attention to one or two matters and ask questions with regard to them. The first is the port of entry at Sault Ste. Marie, which is the closest available to the area which I represent. For many years it has been a port of entry through which thousands of American tourists enter Canada to the great benefit, especially, of northern Ontario. I have had occasion to arrive at this port on many occasions and I must say it is not exactly one of the best in terms of its construction and the

Supply-National Revenue facilities offered. For instance, there is no provision made for protecting the American travellers when they have to open their luggage, and so on: and when the minister thinks of the rainy weather we have been experiencing he will realize what this lack of facilities means. The fences are rusty and broken to a large extent. I must, however, be honest in admitting that there may be a reason why the port of entry is not in a better condition than it is, namely that a new bridge may soon be constructed in the vicinity. This will bring about increased traffic. I trust that the minister will ensure that the proper customs and excise facilities are available when construction of the bridge is undertaken to avoid inconvenience and delay.
The second matter with which I wish to deal is one touched upon by three hon. members of the government. In 1958 the minister introduced certain amendments to the Customs Act and in his opening statement as reported at page 4468 of Hansard of September 2 that year said:
The present law is adequate to deal with most cases of dumping or distress selling, but does not provide a safeguard against sales at prices below cost-plus.
It was the minister's opinion at that time that the law was adequate to deal with most cases of dumping but he wanted to take care of cost-plus sales. I should like the minister to tell us something about the effect of the amendments on the Canadian manufacturing industry and give us figures relating to imports under the new amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to deal with two or three points but before doing so I wish to compliment the minister and the department. This is one of the most efficient and competent departments of government with which I have had the pleasure to deal. It has one of the best deputy ministers who is to be congratulated in another sphere altogether.
What about the poor minister?

All in all there is little one can say in criticism of the department. What I intend to say is not by way of criticism at all. I merely wish to remind the department of a few matters they have under consideration and ask the minister if he would comment.
The first problem I wish to raise is one which I believe was raised in the estimates committee two years ago. It concerns the importation of machinery sold by an importer to a tax exempt user. The specific point I wish to place before the department is this. The original purchaser of machinery for use in logging or a forestry operation, let us say,

is able to have his machinery enter the country exempt of tax. After a certain use of the equipment he may sell it to someone in the construction industry for road building purposes and it becomes taxable. The department has always gone back to the original importer of the equipment for the amount of sales tax which is due on the reduced value of the machinery. The original importer has no control whatever over this equipment. I believe a suggestion was made that the actual sales tax exemption certificate should be in the form of a contract between the department and the original purchaser and any succeeding purchaser and the liability for the payment of any sales tax should rest on the purchaser who purchased the machine for use in a taxable industry. It is not fair at all in my opinion that the original importer of this equipment could be liable for actions over which he has no control. I understand that from the administrative point of view it is much easier to handle the problem this way but it is not right and I believe it should be changed.
The second item I wish to raise does not really come within the purview of the department but should come within its sphere. It has to do with the sale of United States war surplus equipment on which an arbitrary excise and customs figure of 16 or 17 per cent has been set to offset the fact that the equipment came into the country duty free when used on a United States base. Any ordinary secondhand machinery coming into the country will be assessed by the department at what they consider to be its proper value. Sales tax, if applicable, and duty will be levied on the assessed value. You may buy a machine in the United States for $500 but if the price of that machine in a similar condition here happens to be about $2,000 you will be taxed accordingly. These war surplus sales are disturbing to the economy. The United States economy is greater than ours and the people of the United States will not allow these machines to re-enter their country. An agreement was made some time ago between the governments of Canada and the United States. This equipment is sold by war assets. You may have the most ridiculous sales figure. The 16 and 17 per cent is paid on the actual sales figure and not on the assessed value as the department might assess it. That agreement should be changed. I would like to see us cut out the dumping of war surplus material but if this is not possible the taxation on such equipment should be on the same basis as on any other equipment sold to users in this country.

The third problem with which I wish to deal relates to the importation by manufacturers in Canada of United States components and the application of sales tax to the finished product either as assembled or made up from Canadian manufactured components or those plus United States components to make up a certain article. The deputy minister will be familiar with one article concerning which I have been in touch with him. The application of the sales tax is on the finished price, the factory cost as far as the Canadian manufacturer is concerned.
The importer importing an identical article completely made up in a foreign country will pay sales tax on the value at the border. He does not pay sales tax on his profit as the Canadian manufacturer has to do. He does not pay sales tax on transportation and other incidental costs incurred by the Canadian manufacturer. The importer does not pay sales tax on those costs but only as at the border point.
In effect the application of sales tax in this instance is less on a fully manufactured imported article than it is on a Canadian manufactured article which comprises imported parts and parts of Canadian manufacture. The Canadian manufacturer, as far as that part of his cost involving taxation is concerned, is at a price disadvantage as compared to a straight importer of a similar article.
They are not major points; they are not going to put anybody out of business but each of the three points I have brought forward, I think, is in its own way relatively important and deserves consideration from the department as to how it may reasonably be able to correct what is not exactly discrimination but different treatment of one person as opposed to another.

I shall be very brief in my remarks on the minister's estimates but I do first of all wish to express my appreciation of the courtesies extended to me by the minister and the promptness with which he and officials have dealt with any-and there have been a few-complaints that I have had to bring to their attention. However, on occasion the minister has been rather snappy on the orders of the day when answering my questions.
I also wish to express the same sentiments with respect to the deputy minister who is the most popular man I have ever known whose chief occupation in life is taking money away from people. At the same time, I wish to extend compliments to the other senior officials.
Supply-National Revenue
While I am in this mood I might say that I was talking quite recently to a long term employee of the minister's department connected with customs who retired a few years ago and who wished me to extend his kind regards and best wishes to the senior officials of the department. I refer to Mr. Warren Crowe, who has retired under some of the most happy circumstances that I had ever known. He owns a gold mine and spends part of the year mining gold and the rest of the time hunting and fishing and visiting the pioneers of the district. I think this is a very fine way to spend one's retirement.
So far as the local staffs at Nelway and Waneta and Patterson are concerned, I have not had a single complaint. Everyone in the district speaks of the general satisfaction with the way in which the staff services these various ports. However, I do want to bring to the minister's attention the fact that they work long hours to do that. I have had to tell this story before. I have been asked by people in the district to remind the minister again of the local circumstances. People generally are looking forward to the time when the service will be a 24-hour service. I fully appreciate the fact that there is some difficulty in making arrangements with the opposite numbers on the United States side of the line, but people in our district think 24-hour service is justified in view of the income collected at two of the ports, particularly in relation to the income collected at some other ports which have 24-hour service along the international boundary of British Columbia. I should appreciate the minister's informing the house just what the situation is at this time with respect to the possibilities of getting 24-hour service at Nelway and Patterson in fairness to the public and staff.
The other point I wish to bring to his attention is the question of water traffic on the Columbia which is increasing every year. Some years ago arrangements were made for United States citizens using small craft coming up the Columbia from as far south as Portland and going as far north as Revel-stoke to report at Trail. This was a very wise move because the small boats had to take a chance with some very swift water and in one case some whirlpools, and the occupants then travel through the woods for half a mile to try to find the customs office at Waneta. I have talked to a number of people on this question and I suggest that we are getting more and more people and strangers coming in from as far south as Portland. Many of the Spokane and Seattle people know the river quite well, but other people do not. I suggest the department would be

Supply-National Revenue well advised to have a prominent sign erected at the appropriate place near the international boundary, on the side of the river which the craft use in coming up from the United States, pointing out to them that Trail is the port of call and is so many miles from the border. We have had some cases of people not knowing exactly how far they need to go, and thus attempting to land at Waneta.
These are the only two matters I have to bring to the attention of the minister at this time.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say just a few words about these estimates, the minister and his most co-operative department. Today we were honoured with a few remarks by the minister, remarks which were short but certainly to the point. When one visits his office one is accorded the same type of businesslike treatment which is so much appreciated by hon. members. The minister possesses a great deal of business acumen which is so necessary in operating a huge department such as he must administer, and particularly when he and his officials must work so closely with other business houses throughout the country. He also possesses the great faculty of being able to get things done. One might say he is an expediter and a trouble shooter.
I am sure that this businesslike approach has removed many of the headaches which have plagued and which possibly will continue to plague departments such as his. Administrators such as the minister can bring about great savings to the country.
I always like to hear the minister speak in the house. As he towers above the desk so he must tower over the workload which is daily before his office. I think it can be fairly said that the minister has the ability to bring about team effort in his department. I know it has been a pleasure for me to do constituency work with his deputy minister and with other officials in his department.
May I say in passing in regard to Mr. Sim that he is on the executive of one of the local community clubs, and this in itself is a good thing because not only can he do a good job for the community but he can be a good will ambassador for his department. May I suggest to the minister that wherever possible he should encourage his division heads and others in his department to belong to local community clubs in order the better to get to know the problems of the particular area.
Maybe at this point I could make one constructive suggestion with respect to the customs end of the minister's department. I have been aware for some time of what has been

done in the United States immigration and customs service with respect to opening offices in Canada. For example, when one goes from Montreal to New York city one clears customs at the United States customs and immigration office in Montreal so that when one leaves the plane in New York city there is no further formality at that end at all. Therefore travellers are able to avoid a great deal of unnecessary delay at the other end. If that system could be extended to Seattle, for instance, for the benefit of passengers northbound to Canada, passengers could then descend from their planes at Vancouver having already cleared customs and immigration and there would be a great saving in time.
I also wish to compliment the minister upon the efficiency with which the customs officers go about their duties at the various border points across the country. People entering Canada from the United States meet these men first and they can certainly help to create a fair climate and do a great deal in the way of building up good will for Canada. There is no sense in spending a great deal of money in the United States to encourage more tourists to come to Canada if they are met at the border with a wall of indifference. That is not the case at the present time and, in all fairness, has not been for a long time. I wish to compliment the minister and his staff in that regard.
I hope that in due course the minister will be able to make a trip to Vancouver and call at the various border points in the west. We have not had a visit by him for some time but perhaps in due course he will make such a visit in order to see the western border points. As I have to go to a committee, I should like to crave the indulgence of hon. members in order to touch upon the C.B.C. briefly.

speechtext: I suggest it would be preferable if the hon. member would wait until the item for the C.B.C. is called. I know that many other hon. members would like to discuss the item and I think it would mean a more orderly discussion.

That is quite all right. I will abide by your ruling. Before I resume my seat, may I also say to the minister's parliamentary secretary that we appreciate the cooperative spirit he has shown toward members of the house and that he in turn is a great asset to the minister's department.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I want to be clear in my own mind. We are dealing with the collection agency of the government, not the tax imposing agency, and I think that the hon. member is making a speech in regard to matters with which this department has nothing to do.

On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, may I submit that when I tried
Supply-National Revenue to introduce this very subject on a previous occasion the Speaker of the house said there would be other occasions on which to discuss it, and certainly this is the occasion. I continue:
To a vast majority of the owners in Canada a motor car can no longer be regarded as a luxury, but in the light of modern conditions must be regarded as a necessity. However, our tax legislation takes no account whatever of that fact. The burden which this tax has placed upon the automotive industry in Canada and indeed the acute way in which it has been making itself felt latterly are well known to every hon. member of the house. We have on every hand evidence of the increasing state of disorganization in motor car sales right across Canada.
The automotive industry is a major employer of labour in Canada.
That is what I have repeated over and over again, and the Minister of Finance agrees with me. No one disputes the fact that it is an industry which is essential to the well being and development of our country.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I did not rule on the point of order raised by the hon. member for Regina City. I may say that since the hon. member started his speech I have had some concern about the relevancy of his comments. I know that I allowed the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm to speak briefly on the question of customs taxes on tobacco. But I do not think it would be relevant at this point in the discussion of the estimates of the Department of National Revenue to discuss in such detail as the hon. member is attempting the excise tax on automobiles. It seems to me that this is a matter which would have been more properly discussed during the budget debate.
I do not want the hon. member to feel that I am trying to prevent him from continuing his speech. However, I do believe that he should try to be as brief as possible in his discussion of this question, otherwise we will have a repetition of the budget debate. As hon. members realize, the Minister of National Revenue is only charged with the collection of this tax. There is nothing he can do, personally, in connection with the request the hon. member is making. It is a matter either for the government as a whole or for the Minister of Finance. I think, strictly speaking, the hon. member's remarks would be more relevant to the budget debate.

May I ask for clarification of this matter? Before this item carries I think I should reply to some of the questions which have been asked and some of the problems which have been raised. As the hon. member for Laurier suggested a moment ago, there have been many of them, and if I do not attempt to deal with them all I am sure hon. members will not think it is a matter of discourtesy. I will try to refer to some of those which I think have been the more important ones and on which perhaps some explanation is necessary.
The hon. member for Hamilton South raised, as did many other members, including the member for Laurier, the question of textiles and the impact of imports on the textile industry. The hon. member for Hamilton South dealt at some length with the United States subsidy which is paid to cotton producers in the United States and suggested, as have many others here today and elsewhere, that this was a form of subsidization of the textiles which are imported here and is one on which we should impose dumping duty, or deal with in some other way. There is no doubt there is a subsidy paid in the

Supply-National Revenue United States on raw cotton; it is part of the statute law of that country. Incidentally, although the effects here may sometimes be as have been suggested, we also have to realize that cotton is bought by our manufacturers and, by our producers, at cheaper than it otherwise would be because of the fact the subsidy is paid on the cotton which is grown in the United States.
Now what may be termed dumping, of course, is an exercise in semantics. There is dumping in the popular mind and I think there is a misapprehension in the country and in this house that when goods are sold at a price lower than we produce them here, or at a price which seems to us to be low, that is immediately said to be dumping. Whatever may be the moral justification for that, and I think there is one sometimes, there is no legal justification for it unless the technical terms of the statute and of the law are met.
The term is, of course, as most hon. members know, that we are governed by the current market price in the country of origin. Given a free market and normal trading conditions, if that price is lower than ours it is still the free market price. That is the value which we have to impose on the goods, and it is not dumping. I think there is perhaps some misapprehension in the mind of the hon. member for Laurier and others. We are always hearing about dumping as if everybody dumped into this country. If they are selling goods a little bit cheaper than we are selling them in the open market here, then, unfortunate as that may be to some producers, that is not dumping under the act. We can only impose a dumping duty when the goods are sold here at a lower price than the open market price in the country of origin.
The department has had a number of complaints about the matter of subsidization. It has been suggested to us by textile manufacturers that subsidization is going on. The hon. member for Hamilton South read what I took to be a letter from a producer in the United States indicating that certain moneys were being kept there for the importer. If the money comes into Canada it is then something with which we can deal very easily but if there is money paid and it does not come into Canada it is questionable what is our legal position. All I can say is that the department has investigated this matter time and time again, has dealt with it and is attempting to deal with it in every possible way consistent with the law, and we would welcome any information or any co-operation which would assist us to deal further with this difficult problem.
As has been pointed out by various members, there is no question that the textile

I want to mention casually and very briefly some of the things we have done in connection with the textile industry and without enumerating too much. The appraisers on the headquarters staff in Ottawa are travelling all the time to various portions of the United States for the purpose of investigating and checking on values, complaints and so forth.
With respect to the matter of invoicing, we have also tightened up in that regard. To assist in the detection of undervaluation, exporters are now required to show technical information on invoices and to attach samples of the goods to the invoice so that we can check on those samples and make sure they are in keeping with the invoice which purports to cover them. We have issued other instructions to our officers dealing with these matters. We have given a course on textile cost accounting to all our appraisers. They have been instructed in these matters and we believe they are thoroughly efficient and are carrying out the law as it is today to the limit of the extent to which it can be enforced and maintained.
Supply-National Revenue
We did bring seconds within the purview of the Customs Act in so far as dumping is concerned. Heretofore seconds were not included. Approximately a year ago we brought seconds under the act by order in council to protect against dumping. Seconds of course, comprise a very substantial portion of our textile imports because seconds from the United States are a very good class of goods. They are a substantial portion of our imports and by bringing them within the purview of the act we have improved the situation materially.
Reference was made by the hon. member for Laurier to importations from Japan and China and the action taken by the Minister of Finance in co-operation with the Japanese government with respect to the acceptance of quotas by that government. There is nothing much I need to say on that matter in addition to what has been said by the Minister of Finance. The department is administering the provision. I have imposed dumping duties on textiles from China. We have imposed very heavy duties against the protests, of course, of various importers who thought their valuations would be accepted but we refused to accept them. We are still continuing that course of action.
There are other matters, of course, such as discounts. We started to check on this matter a year or so ago and we found that discounts being authorized on imports of textiles were very substantial. As I reported to the house some time ago, we revised these discounts. We issued a new bulletin, appraisers' bulletin No. 12, and whereas discounts had run as high as 20, 25 or 30 per cent we reduced them substantially on the great majority of imports. On cotton sheets, cotton pillow cases, twill and clothing sateen we reduced the discount in each case to a maximum of 5 per cent and 10 per cent on denim. This has made a substantial contribution to the textile industry.
Far be it from me to say that the condition of the industry is good. It is not, and it is a matter which is causing us concern at all times. However, I can say this without fear of contradiction, that if it had not been for some of the steps we have taken and the action which this department has carried out as well as the investigations which are constantly carried out, bad as the condition of the industry is today, it would be infinitely worse if those actions had not been taken.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It could hardly be worse in certain areas.

I am not trying to justify the situation. This is a matter over which this department has no control. We have administered the law to the extent that it is

Supply-National Revenue humanly possible in order to give the industry all the safeguards and protection which it could possibly receive.
The hon. member for Port Arthur raised a perennial question about which we have had many interesting discussions, the question of censorship. He asked if new instructions had been sent out to our port officers recently in connection with this matter. I can tell him no such instructions have gone out. The administration is exactly the same as it was at that time. It is an interesting problem as to what our position will be as decisions come out, become codified and the law becomes clear. We welcome that because it is a nasty situation in which one finds himself as the ultimate, in one sense, censor. It must be remembered that this only applies to periodicals coming across the border. It does not apply to anything printed in this country. It does not apply to anything on sale in the bookstores. It is only when books come through the customs house that we have a responsibility, and we are attempting to carry it out in the best way possible.
If I may summarize, then, there has been no change at all in the work of the minister's officials in this particular field as a result of the legislative change last year?

No, the legislative change last year was concerned with administration within Canada. Our responsibility is for goods coming into the country. Obviously there has to be a close correlation between the two. We have made no change in the instructions issued to our officials up to the present time.

May I ask another question before the minister proceeds. Am I not correct in my recollection that a couple of sessions ago the minister expressed a rather determined desire to free himself from this responsibility of censorship? Can he tell the committee whether any progress has been made toward that desirable objective?

I am afraid the progress has not been as great as the minister would like. There have been discussions between my department and the Department of Justice and the respective ministers thereof. I was very hopeful that some section could be worked out which would relieve this department entirely of any responsibility in connection with the matter. I am told that this is a matter of common practice, of common law, and I guess virtually every jurisdiction in the world which has a customs act has to deal with this problem. Every once in a while we do get books coming through customs and if you dropped them on the floor you


would have to clean them up with a shovel. These items do not present a great deal of difficulty. Beyond these the activities of the department have been of a very limited nature and I trust they will always continue to be.

The minister will recall the strong criticism levelled at his predecessor because the government of that day was not able to get rid of that responsibility which the minister of national revenue was exercising. Indeed, he was accused of being rather happy in the exercise of it, which was not true. It did add to his library, but I do not know whether it has served to add to the minister's library?

No, I have been very careful, I must say, as to the ultimate destination of these books. I can assure you that they are all returned to the deputy minister, and no further inquiry is made. Of course, they only come to me when they have the signature of the deputy minister. In the first place they come through the port officials and finally to the deputy minister. If there is any disagreement about the decision then the book comes to me. I sometimes read of very interesting books in the newspapers and wonder why they do not get to my desk, and I sometimes wonder what would happen if they did. However, it is sometimes my unpleasant responsibility to read these books.
Is it not regrettably true that the deputy minister is soon to acquire a lot of time which he could use for this purpose?

I will not pass any judgment on that, Mr. Chairman.
I think, too, the hon. member for Port Arthur raised a question about the closing of some ports. He could not understand why the revenue in some cases appeared to be very small and yet the ports would be kept open, whereas in other cases the revenue seemed to be larger and the ports were closed. It is very difficult to lay down any hard and fast rule with respect to these matters. The matter of port administration is always under review. It is true that we have closed some ports, and it is true that we will probably close some more. I get recommendations from time to time from our committee on port administration dealing with these matters, and one has to face these facts.
I pointed out earlier the reduction we had made in our expenditures. This has not been accomplished to any great extent by the closing of ports, but it is in keeping with the efficiency with which we have carried out this division of our responsibility and sometimes, unfortunately, we have to do that. One cannot measure it entirely, although it is a

big yardstick, by the dollars received. There is the question of proximity to other ports. It may be that people would have to travel great distances if there were not a port at a certain place, and that is a factor. There is also the factor of security arrangements and the deterrent. If there were not a port in a certain place and there were a road leading from one country to another which was not under surveillance at all I suspect the amount of travel on that particular road would increase. It is necessary sometimes, therefore, to have ports in areas which do not, in themselves, bring in a great deal of money. However, if those ports were not there we would perhaps lose a great deal more money.
I should like to remind the minister that the examples I gave were not of ports on boundaries or international waters, so one part of the minister's reply does not apply.

excise tax on cars, a matter also referred to by one or two other hon. members. That again is a matter for the Minister of Finance. I administer the tax; I collect it, but it is not a matter which comes within the purview of this department and any discussion of that matter should be raised on the estimates of the Minister of Finance.
The hon. member for Fort William also complained about a step which this department took in, shall we say, making Fort William, as he termed it, an outport of Port Arthur. It is true we did make a change there. The collector at Fort William had reached retirement age and had retired; there was competent staff there and we all know the proximity of Fort William and Port Arthur. It certainly does not affect the efficiency of the department or the service. It may be a matter I suppose of some local pride that the port is now the port of Port Arthur and that Fort William is not a port but an outport of Port Arthur; 1 think that would be the technical description. But as I say the efficiency of the service to the public is exactly the same as before.
The hon. member for Waterloo North raised the matter of excise. There has been a great deal of consolidation in excise offices. We are trying to consolidate them and give better service by centralizing them across Canada instead of having excise offices in most of our ports. Outside of one area about which some complaints have been received we are effecting distinct economies and think we are giving a better service, because in this highly technical field it is desirable to have senior and competent officials in charge of administration.
The hon. member for Grey-Bruce raised again the question of marking goods. He has raised it privately with me before and I think I might say that some progress has been made there.
The hon. member for Laurier raised the problem about the Canadian association of income tax employees, Montreal branch. He was not in the committee when we started our discussion and apparently assumed we were covering both branches of the family, but we were only dealing with customs and excise; however, I will refer to this matter when we come to the taxation branch.
The hon. member for Moose Mountain raised the question of coal machinery. That machinery was brought in on a one sixtieth basis and presents this problem but we are going to study it again.
The hon. member for York North raised the question of "Made in Canada". I think the inference was that perhaps we should not have a "Made in Canada" ruling or that it

was a difficult one to administer. We do have more and more requests for that. One of my problems every week is to deal with applications for "Made in Canada" rulings and it is one without which we could not administer the features of the dumping act and many others.
The hon. member for Hull raised the question of the E.24 being in French and English and thought that we could combine the two languages on the one form. We are certainly prepared to take a look at that although I think my officials would say rather whimsically that they have enough trouble with the form in just one language and that if we had both languages on the form the confusion would be more confounded and the minister more damned than at the present time for having to enforce that section. But we will look at the matter.
I think that covers the matters raised.
I did ask a question about the Russian treaty and the procedures for valuations under that treaty.

Yes. The Leader of the Opposition asked about the procedures which would be followed with respect to goods to be imported from Russia pursuant to the Russian trade treaty. The procedure there is one which is the normal procedure of the department, what we call the third country procedure. In the case of Russia we are dealing with a state-controlled nation where free marketing as we know it does not exist. Therefore we cannot estimate the value for duty purposes in the way we would with respect to goods imported from other countries. So the responsibility falls upon the Minister of National Revenue to devise a method whereby value for duty may be determined, and I propose dealing with imports from Russia and similar countries by invoking the third nation principle; to try to fix a valuation based on that of a similar product from a country where conditions are as comparable with those that obtain in Russia as possible.
There has been a great deal of misunderstanding about this. It has been suggested that the Minister of Trade and Commerce made a deal about oil. One would think from some of the things that have been said that this country is being flooded with Russian oil and Russian motor cars. As a matter of fact, there is not a gallon of Russian oil in the country, and outside the members of the diplomatic corps who may have one or two Russian cars, there is not a Russian car in the whole country.
There have been discussions between my officials and prospective importers and with
79951-0-369J
Supply-National Revenue officials of the Russian embassy here as to what method would be followed. That situation has been clarified, but at the moment there are no goods of that nature being brought in, either cars or gas, and no value for duty has yet been assessed by officials of my department.

May I ask the minister if the procedures which he says his department is working out will be influenced in any way by the obligation in the new treaty to import -I forget what the actual figures are-about half as much in valuation as we export. Will that have any influence on the procedure? Further, am I right in saying that at the present time there is no change from previous procedures with regard to Russia? May I finally ask the minister whether it is contemplated that an official of the Department of National Revenue should be stationed in Moscow for this purpose?

There has been no change in the procedure whatsoever. Of course, attention has to be given to all facets of every problem but certainly in fixing this valuation we have to be guided by the facts as we find them and by the values which exist in comparable areas, if comparable areas can be found, as I think they can. Much as we may want to encourage an increase in trade -and we would be very pleased to see such an increase-we cannot allow that to influence us in fixing values on the basis of a proper comparison. On the advice of my officials I will try to find markets where the conditions are as closely comparable as is possible to find with conditions existing in whatever part of Russia these goods may originate.
As far as the sending of an official to Moscow is concerned, that matter has not yet arisen. It may be necessary to do so, but we have no immediate intention of doing so. (Translation):

Mr. Chairman, the present plight of the confectionery and pure chocolate industry in Canada has been brought to the attention of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), and I thought he would have given us the views of his department on the matter, because I know the minister is aware that that industry is facing serious competition from importers who are putting chocolate products on the market at a price lower than the costs to Canadian manufacturers. Might not the minister, with the

Supply-National Revenue co-operation of his officials, investigate the situation with a view to eliminating the 11 per cent tax on Canadian made confectionery and chocolate products, which raises the cost of such products?
I also wonder whether the minister would consider raising the tariff on the entry of such products, so as to enable-
(Text):

speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member is talking about raising or lowering tariffs. That does not come under this department, but under the Department of Finance.
I thought that since questions of this kind were permitted before I would be allowed to produce them myself.

In that case, Mr. Chairman, perhaps the minister might consider classifying chocolates and candy as foods rather than luxuries. This would in effect remove the 11 per cent tax that weights upon that Canadian industry.
One confectionery manufacturer, in my constituency, is in serious trouble because of that tariff. He employs a few hundred workers, and I think that Canadian manufacturers of confectionery provide jobs for thousands of people across the country.
